01-001.json.summary: After a bow to Narayana, Nara, Sarasvati and Vishnu in his tortoise form (Kurma), the sages of the Naimisha forest ask Suta Romaharshana, Vyasa's pupil, to tell them the Kurma Purana. Suta agrees, warning that it must be told only to faithful, calm, righteous twice-born men, never to an unbeliever. He gives the five marks of a Purana, lists the eighteen Puranas and eighteen minor Puranas, and says the Kurma is the fifteenth, with four collections; this one, the Brahmi, has six thousand verses. When gods and demons churned the ocean of milk, Vishnu as a tortoise held up Mount Mandara, and the goddess Shri (Lakshmi) rose and was taken by him. Asked by Narada, Indra and the sages who she is, Vishnu says she is his own supreme power and Maya (power of illusion), the threefold nature that bewitches the world and that no one can cross. To show who can cross her, he tells of Indradyumna: once a king who heard this Purana from Kurma and took refuge in him, he was promised rebirth as a Brahmin remembering his past life. Born so, he worshipped Vishnu with vows and fasts; Shri appeared and said she is one with Narayana and has no power over those who worship the Lord with knowledge and action. Vishnu then appeared, Indradyumna praised him, and at his touch knew the highest truth. Vishnu taught that people keeping their class and life-stage duties must worship the great Lord (Maheshvara) with knowledge and devotion, see the world as Maya, and practise one of three meditations: on Vishnu, on the manifest world, or on Brahman beyond the qualities. Indradyumna asked about duties, creation, the Manus, dynasties, holy places and the shape of the earth; Kurma told him all and vanished. Indradyumna renounced everything, reached the final meditation, flew to Mount Manasottara where Brahma embraced him, and a light from his body passed through the sun to Vishnu's highest state, liberation. Suta says Kurma later told this whole Purana to the sages in Indra's presence; hearing even one chapter frees one from all sins.

01-002.json.summary: Kurma starts telling the sages what he taught Indradyumna. In the beginning only he, Narayana, existed, asleep on the serpent bed. When he woke, Brahma was born from his grace, Rudra with the trident from his anger, and Shri, the great Maya and root nature, came to sit beside him. At Brahma's request he told Shri to bewitch gods, demons and men so creation would grow, but to keep away from the self-controlled, the truthful, those devoted to knowledge and yoga, Veda-knowers, worshippers of Maheshvara, those who repeat Om and the Rudra prayers, and all who keep their duty; so Lakshmi, who gives wealth, wisdom and strength, should be worshipped. Brahma created his nine mind-born sons (Marichi, Bhrigu, Angiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, Daksha, Atri and Vasishtha), the Brahmins from his mouth, Kshatriyas from his arms, Vaishyas from his thighs and Shudras from his feet, and the four Vedas, his eternal speech. The text says scriptures outside the Veda are fruitless and lead to darkness. When people's first purity faded through desire and hatred, Brahma set up livelihood by work, and Svayambhuva Manu declared the duties: the Brahmin's six acts (sacrificing, officiating, giving, receiving, teaching, studying), the Kshatriya's ruling and fighting, the Vaishya's farming, and the Shudra's service to the twice-born, with crafts. The four life stages and their duties follow; the householder, on whom the others live, is called the best. Dharma brings wealth, pleasure and liberation, so wealth and pleasure against dharma must be given up, and only inward-turned action done with knowledge leads to the highest state. Common duties for all classes are listed (patience, kindness, truth, non-violence and others), and each class and stage has its own heavenly world. Asked about a fifth stage for yogis, Kurma says the yogi is a renunciant, and he describes kinds of students, householders, forest dwellers and renunciants. Brahma creates, Vishnu protects and Shiva destroys; they are three forms of one Supreme, and Narayana and Mahadeva are not truly different. Shiva's devotees wear three lines of white ash (tripundra) on the forehead, Narayana's a trident mark, Brahma's a round mark (tilaka); one who worships them all his life by his duties soon reaches their lasting home.

01-003.json.summary: Kurma tells the sages the order of the life stages: student, householder, forest dweller and renunciant, with exceptions. A student with deep knowledge and detachment may renounce at once; otherwise one should marry, sacrifice and have sons before renouncing, unless detachment is so strong that one cannot stay at home. One may also renounce from the forest stage, and one who has gone to the forest must not return home. Renunciation follows an offering to Prajapati or Agni; even the blind, lame or poor may renounce if detached, but one who renounces without detachment falls. One may also stay faithfully in one stage until death and reach immortality. Kurma then teaches the offering of action to Brahman (brahmarpana): to think that Brahman gives, receives and is the gift, or 'I am not the doer', or to give up the fruits of acts to the Lord. Duties done without attachment lead to liberation, while even daily rites done for their fruit bind. Action destroys past sins and clears the mind, and action joined with knowledge leads to yoga; so in any stage one should act to please the Lord, reach freedom from action, be freed while alive, see Maheshvara, the supreme Brahman, and merge in him. No one reaches perfection by going beyond this fourfold order.

01-004.json.summary: The sages ask Kurma how the world arises, where it dissolves and who rules it. He says Maheshvara is the supreme unmanifest ruler. The unmanifest cause, Pradhana or Prakriti (primal nature), is eternal, without sound, touch, form, taste or smell, and made of the three qualities. While the qualities are in balance there is dissolution, Brahma's night; creation is his day. At night's end the Lord enters nature and spirit and stirs them, as spring wind stirs the world, being both the stirrer and the stirred. From this came Mahat (the great principle), then the threefold ego (ahamkara). From these came the mind, the ten senses and their gods, and the subtle and gross elements in order (sound and space, touch and air, form and fire, taste and water, smell and earth), each later element holding the qualities of those before. Joined together, these produced a cosmic egg floating on water, in which Brahma (Hiranyagarbha), the first embodied being, arose; Meru was its inner skin, the mountains its outer skin and the oceans its fluid, and in it were all the worlds and beings. Seven coverings surround the egg, each ten times larger: water, fire, air, space, ego, Mahat and the unmanifest. With the quality of passion the Lord creates as Brahma, with goodness he protects as Vishnu, and with darkness he destroys as Rudra, one Mahadeva standing in three. The chapter explains his names: Aja because unborn, Prajapati as protector of creatures, Ishvara as controller, Hari as remover, Narayana as the refuge of men, Hara as remover of worldly life, Vishnu as all-pervading, Shiva as pure, Taraka as the one who carries beings across sorrow. The whole world is Brahman, and Kurma says he will next describe Brahma's creation.

01-005.json.summary: Kurma explains the measure of time. Fifteen blinks make a kashtha, thirty kashthas a kala, thirty kalas a muhurta, thirty muhurtas a day and night, thirty days a month, and twelve months a year; the sun's southern half-year is a night of the gods and the northern half-year their day. In divine years the Krita age lasts 4,000, the Treta 3,000, the Dvapara 2,000 and the Kali (Tishya) 1,000, each with dawn and dusk periods of a tenth of that length on each side, making 12,000 for the four ages. Seventy-one sets of four ages make a Manu period (manvantara), and fourteen Manus, from Svayambhuva to the Savarnis, rule the seven-continent earth in one day of Brahma. A thousand sets of four ages make a kalpa, Brahma's day, and his night is as long; 360 such days make his year, and a hundred years his life, made of two halves (parardhas). At its end all beings, with Brahma, Narayana and Shiva, dissolve into nature, and by time arise again. Time is the beginningless, ageless Lord, Maheshvara; there are many Brahmas, Rudras and Narayanas, but one Lord, Time. Half of Brahma's life has passed; the last kalpa was the Padma, and the present one is the Varaha (boar) kalpa, which Kurma will now describe.

01-006.json.summary: Kurma says that in the beginning there was only a dark, endless ocean in which all things had perished. Brahma, called Narayana, thousand-headed, thousand-eyed and golden, slept on the waters; a verse explains that the waters are called nara and he is Narayana because they are his resting place (ayana). After a night of a thousand ages he took up the role of creator. Knowing the earth lay sunk in the waters, he took the form of a boar (Varaha), made of the Veda, entered the lower world and lifted the earth on his tusk. The siddhas and sages of Janaloka praised him with a hymn, bowing to him as Brahma, Hiranyagarbha, Vasudeva, Vishnu and Narayana, the five elements, root nature and Maya, the Boar and the Fish, and asked him to protect the world he created and will absorb. Pleased with Sanaka and the others, he set the earth in place, where it floats on the waters like a boat and does not sink because of its size, gave up the boar form, levelled the earth, gathered on it the mountains burned in the former creation, and turned his mind to creating beings.

01-007.json.summary: Kurma describes Brahma's creation. First a creation made without thought arose, full of darkness: ignorance in five forms. Then came the unmoving things such as mountains and trees, shut in by darkness; then animals, whose stream runs sideways; then the gods, full of goodness and light; then human beings, who have light but also passion and suffering, yet can reach the goal; then the bhutas. Kurma counts nine creations in all, the first three (Mahat, the elements, the senses) being natural and made without thought, and the ninth the Kaumara. Brahma's first mind-born sons, Sanaka, Sanatana, Sanandana, Ribhu and Sanatkumara, were detached yogis and refused to create. Brahma, bewildered, did penance in vain; from his sorrow came anger and tears, and from his frowning forehead Mahadeva, the blue-red one (Nilalohita), was born. Asked to create, Shiva made Rudras like himself, three-eyed and fearless, but refused to create beings subject to old age and death and told Brahma to make such beings himself. Brahma then made the powers ruling places and times, and the householder sages from parts of his body and breaths: Daksha, Marichi, Angiras, Bhrigu, Atri, Dharma, Samkalpa, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu and Vasishtha. Taking different bodies, he created demons from his loins (that body became night), gods from his mouth (day), ancestors (twilight), humans from a body of passion (moonlight, the dawn), and Rakshasas, Yakshas, serpents and Gandharvas from darkness and hunger. Birds, sheep, goats, cows, horses, elephants and other animals came from parts of his body and plants from his hair, and the Vedic metres, hymns and sacrifices from his four mouths, east, south, west and north in turn. Each being takes up again the gentle or cruel, true or false actions it had in the former creation, and the Lord gives them their names and roles from the words of the Veda, the same at each new creation, as the signs of each season return in turn.

01-008.json.summary: Kurma continues. When the beings did not multiply, Brahma grew sad; he drove out the darkness in himself, and from it were born wrongdoing (adharma) and violence (himsa). He then divided his body into a man and a woman: the man, Viraj, was Svayambhuva Manu, and the woman was Shatarupa, a yogini who by hard penance won Manu as husband. They had two sons, Priyavrata and Uttanapada, and two daughters: Prasuti, given to Daksha, and Akuti, given to Ruchi. From Akuti came Yajna (sacrifice) and Dakshina (the sacrificial fee), whose twelve sons were the Yama gods. Daksha and Prasuti had twenty-four daughters. Thirteen, such as Shraddha (faith), Lakshmi, Dhriti (steadiness), Medha (wisdom), Lajja (modesty), Shanti (peace) and Kirti (fame), married Dharma; the other eleven, Khyati, Sati, Sambhuti, Smriti, Priti, Kshama, Santati, Anasuya, Urja, Svaha and Svadha, married Bhrigu, Bhava (Shiva), Marichi, Angiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, Atri, Vasishtha, Agni and the ancestors. Dharma's children are good qualities, such as Kama (desire) from Faith, Santosha (contentment), Shama (calm), Vinaya (humility), Sukha (happiness) and Yasha (glory); this line ends in happiness. From Adharma came Himsa, who bore Deceit and Falsehood; from these came Fear, Hell, Maya and Pain, and from them Death and Sorrow, and from Death came disease, old age, grief, craving and anger. These all end in sorrow, have no wives or sons, and form the dark creation that keeps dharma in check.

01-009.json.summary: Suta says Narada and the sages ask how Shiva, born first, became Brahma's son, and how Brahma became lotus-born. Kurma explains. At the end of the last kalpa Narayana slept alone on the serpent Shesha in the dark ocean, and in play a huge shining lotus grew from his navel. Brahma came, deluded by Maya, woke him and asked who he was. Each claimed to be the source of the worlds; Vishnu entered Brahma's body and saw the three worlds there, then invited Brahma into his own. Brahma found no end inside Vishnu and all doors shut but the navel, and came out through it onto the lotus. Angry, he asked why Vishnu had tried to defeat him; Vishnu said it was only play and asked Brahma to be his son, the lotus-born. Brahma agreed but claimed that he and Vishnu were the only lords. Vishnu warned that this claim would ruin him and told him to take refuge in Maheshvara, and an angry argument followed. Then Shiva appeared to show Brahma grace, three-eyed, with matted hair, trident and a garland of planets and stars. Vishnu told the puzzled Brahma that this is Mahadeva, who creates, keeps and destroys all as Time, who made Brahma and gave him the Vedas, and of whom Vishnu is another form, and gave him divine sight. Brahma took refuge in Shiva as his father and praised him with the Atharvashiras. Shiva, pleased, offered a boon; Brahma asked that Shiva be born as his son, and Shiva agreed, appointing Brahma as first creator with Narayana to care for him. Vishnu asked only for devotion to Shiva. Shiva said the two of them are not truly different: Vishnu is the moon and he the sun, Vishnu night and he day, nature and spirit, Maya and its Lord, power and its holder; yogis see them as one, and no yogi reaches Shiva without relying on Vishnu. Telling Vishnu to protect the world, Shiva went to his own unmanifest home.

01-010.json.summary: Kurma goes on. While Brahma sat on the lotus, two mountain-sized demon brothers, Madhu and Kaitabha, born from Vishnu's ear, came full of anger; at Brahma's request Vishnu sent two beings from himself, and Jishnu killed Kaitabha and Vishnu killed Madhu. Vishnu asked Brahma to come down, as he could not carry him; Brahma entered Vishnu's body and slept on the waters as Narayana in yogic sleep. At dawn he became Brahma again and created Sanandana, Sanaka, Ribhu, Sanatkumara and Sanatana, who, detached, would not create. Vishnu reminded the despairing Brahma of Shiva's promise. Brahma did penance in vain; his tears of anger became bhutas and pretas (ghosts), he gave up his life-breath in rage, and from his mouth Rudra appeared, bright as a thousand suns, crying loudly. Brahma named him Rudra because he cried (rud), and gave him seven more names (Bhava, Sharva, Ishana, Pashupati, Bhima, Ugra, Mahadeva), eight bodies (sun, water, earth, fire, wind, space, the Brahmin who performs sacrifice, and moon), eight wives and eight sons; those who worship the Rudras in these eight places reach the highest state. Shiva created countless Rudras like himself, free of age and death, but refused to create mortal beings, so he stood still and is called Sthanu (the fixed one); ten lasting qualities such as knowledge, detachment, lordship, truth and patience always live in him. Brahma praised him with a long hymn, bowing to him as Time, Rudra, the father of Brahma, the giver of the knowledge of Brahman, and as the cosmic body, sun, fire, moon, wind, Shesha and the dancer at the end of time. Shiva gave Brahma yoga, knowledge and detachment, said he had fulfilled his wish to be his son, and explained that he divides himself as Brahma, from his right side, Vishnu, from his left, and Rudra, from his heart, for creation, protection and destruction, while his highest three-eyed form is beyond them; whenever Brahma thinks of him he will be near. Shiva vanished, and Brahma created the nine sages called the nine Brahmas, and Samkalpa, Dharma and the rest, as told before. The chapter ends in the middle of a sentence.

01-011.json.summary: This is a very short chapter. Kurma says that while Brahma did penance with his mind-born sons, Rudra appeared from his mouth, born of the fire of time, three-eyed, with a trident and a terrible body half woman and half man. Brahma told him to divide himself and vanished in fear. Rudra split into female and male; the male part became the eleven Rudras, such as Kapalisha, who rule the three worlds and serve the gods, and the female part became many powers (shaktis), gentle and fierce, dark and fair, such as Lakshmi, through whom Shiva's power fills the world. At Shiva's command the goddess went to Brahma, who told her to be born as Daksha's daughter; as Sati she was given to Rudra. Later she was born as Parvati, daughter of Himavat and Mena, and again given to Rudra for the good of the gods. She is Maheshvari, half of Shiva's body, whose power only Shankara or Hari truly knows. Kurma closes by saying he has now told how Shiva became Brahma's son and Brahma became lotus-born.

01-012.json.summary: This chapter is the Greatness of the Goddess (Devi Mahatmya). The sages ask who the goddess is who forms half of Shiva's body, and Kurma tells a secret teaching once given by Brahma on Mount Meru. Haimavati is Maheshvara's power (shakti): all-pervading, beyond the qualities, one and many, inseparable from Shiva like light from the sun. She does all the work of the world; her four forms are Shanti, Vidya, Pratishtha and Nivritti. The Lord is Time, who creates and destroys and is ruled by none, and his power is Maya, from which come the powers of knowledge, action and breath. The wise speak of a difference between power and its holder, but yogis see Shiva and Girija as one. Her highest state is the partless, blissful Brahman, so one seeking liberation should take refuge in Parvati. Himavat and Mena did hard penance and she was born as their daughter by her own will. Himavat saw her with four faces, three eyes and eight arms and asked who she was; she said she is the supreme power resting in the Lord, gave him divine sight, and showed her cosmic form, blazing like millions of suns and doomsday fires, with tusks, crown, mace, conch, discus and trident, yet also gentle, with hands, feet and faces everywhere. In fear and joy Himavat praised her with a long hymn of names (called both a thousand and eight thousand names), naming her Uma, Maya, root nature, slayer of the buffalo demon Mahishasura, mother of Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva, Bhavani, Lakshmi, Sarasvati, Gauri, Mahakali, Kaushiki and many more. When he asked her to put away the terrible form, she showed a gentle two-armed form, dark as a blue lotus, smiling and adorned. Relieved, he praised her as the best in every kind (Indra among gods, Vasishtha among sages, Om among secrets, Meru among mountains) and bowed to each of her forms, from the formless one to Narayana, Time, Shesha and Rudra, and asked what he should do. The goddess taught him to worship her supreme form with devotion, sacrifice, penance and gifts, and to do the duties of class and life stage set out in the Veda and smriti, joined with knowledge of the Self, for dharma comes only from the Veda, which is her own power. Brahma made the classes to protect the Vedas and hells for those who neglect their duty. Texts against the Veda end in darkness; she names the Kapala, Pancharatra, Yamala, Vama and Arhata (Jain) teachings as made for delusion, and says the twice-born should not speak with those who delight in them. The law books of Manu and the sages, Vyasa's eighteen Puranas, the minor Puranas and the fourteen branches of knowledge uphold dharma. Those who take refuge in her she frees with the lamp of knowledge; one unable to meditate on her formless form may worship any form his mind can grasp, but liberation and knowledge of Shiva come only through her. She says she was born to Mena after rejecting her father Daksha for insulting Shiva, and that Himavat will give her to Rudra at her choice of husband (svayamvara), so all the gods will honour him. At his request she taught him Maheshvara's yoga in detail, and he gave Parvati to Shiva before the gods. Reading this chapter frees one from all sins and leads beyond Brahma's world to the goddess's home; a twice-born man who repeats her names daily until death, thinking of her in the sun's disc, reaches the supreme Brahman or union with Shiva. Offering each name into the fire three times a day frees one from harm by Putana and other child-seizing spirits and by the planets, and a year of daily repetition with worship of Parvati and Shiva brings great wealth. Kurma says he will next tell of the creation by Bhrigu and the others.

01-013.json.summary: The offspring of Daksha's daughters is the subject here, told by Suta. Bhrigu and Khyati had Lakshmi, beloved of Narayana, and the gods Dhata and Vidhata, who married Meru's daughters; Markandeya descends from their son Mrikandu. Marichi and Sambhuti had Paurnamasa and four daughters; Pulaha and Kshama had Kardama and other sons; Atri and Anasuya had Soma, Durvasas and the yogi Dattatreya; Angiras and Smriti had Sinivali, Kuhu, Raka and Anumati; Pulastya and Priti had Dambhoji, who was Agastya in an earlier age. Kratu had sixty thousand celibate sons, the Valakhilyas, and Vasishtha and Urja had seven sons and a daughter. Svaha bore to Agni, a form of Rudra, three fires: Pavaka (lightning), Pavamana (fire made by rubbing sticks) and Shuchi (the sun); with their descendants they make forty-nine fires, all sharers in sacrifice and marked with three lines of ash. The Pitris (ancestors) are of two kinds, those who do not sacrifice and those who do; Svadha bore them Mena and Vaitarani. Mena bore the mountains Mainaka and Krauncha and the Ganga, and Himavat gained the goddess Maheshvari as his daughter. Suta then turns to the creation of Manu.

01-014.json.summary: Svayambhuva Manu's line begins with his sons Priyavrata and Uttanapada; Uttanapada's son Dhruva won the highest place through devotion to Narayana. The line runs through several kings to Chakshusha Manu, then Anga, Vena and Prithu, who milked the earth for his people. Suta says that at Prithu's sacrifice Hari himself was born as the bard Suta, 'and I am he'; Vyasa taught him the Purana, and bards of his line, who do not study the Veda, live by telling Puranas. Prithu won two sons from Vishnu by penance on Govardhana. His grandson Sushila, turning to renunciation, met the Pashupata sage Shvetashvatara in the Himalaya by the Mandakini; the sage performed the rite of renunciation for him, gave him the knowledge of Ishvara and the Pashupata vow, said Narayana and the gods had worshipped Shiva in that very place, and taught him the mantra beginning 'Agni'. Sushila lived as an ash-covered ascetic on roots and fruits. From Prithu's other son came Prachinabarhis, the ten Prachetases and Daksha, once Brahma's son. That earlier Daksha, wanting more honour than Shiva gave him, scolded his daughter Sati and her husband; Sati burned her body by her own power and was reborn as Himavat's daughter, and Shiva cursed Daksha to be born among warriors and to father a son on his own daughter. Hearing this account destroys sin.

01-015.json.summary: When the sages ask what Daksha did after Shiva's curse, Suta tells of the ruin of his sacrifice at Gangadvara. All the gods came with Vishnu, but Shiva was left out. The sage Dadhicha protested; Daksha said Shiva, the dark, naked, skull-bearing destroyer, has no share, and only Narayana is lord of sacrifice. Deluded by Vishnu's power, the sages sided with Daksha; Brahma vanished, and Dadhicha cursed the Brahmins who helped Daksha to be outside the three Vedas, follow false scriptures and go to hell in the Kali age. At the Goddess's request Shiva created the thousand-headed Virabhadra, and Uma's anger produced Bhadrakali; with thousands of Rudras born from his body hair, Virabhadra demanded Shiva's share. The gods refused, and the Mantras themselves rebuked them and left. Virabhadra burned the hall, threw the priests and the horse into the Ganga, froze Indra's arm, plucked out Bhaga's eyes, broke Pushan's teeth, cut off Agni's hands and tongue, stopped Vishnu's discus and routed Garuda with thousands of Garudas of his own. Brahma calmed him, and Shiva came with Uma. At her request he forgave everyone, saying he must be worshipped in every sacrifice, and promised Daksha leadership of his hosts at the end of the age. Brahma taught Daksha that Vishnu and Rudra are one ('who is Vishnu is Rudra'), and those who see them as different go to hell; Daksha took refuge in Shiva. The cursed sages, born in Kali as haters of Shiva, will be freed at the end of the age by Shiva's grace.

01-016.json.summary: Daksha's sixty daughters and their children open this long chapter, told by Suta. They were given to Dharma, Kashyapa, Soma and others; Dharma's wives bore the Vasus and other god groups, and Kashyapa's wife Aditi bore the twelve Adityas, while Diti bore Hiranyakashipu and Hiranyaksha. Proud of Brahma's boons, Hiranyakashipu oppressed the gods. Vishnu first sent a huge Person on Garuda, whom the demon drove back, and then appeared in his city as Narasimha, half man and half lion. Prahlada, sent to fight him, was beaten, recognised him as Vasudeva and begged his father to submit; the father refused, and Narasimha tore him apart with his claws. Hiranyaksha, crowned by Prahlada, dragged the earth to the underworld until Vishnu as the Boar killed him. Prahlada, cursed by a Brahmin he had failed to honour, lost his devotion for a time, fought Vishnu, was beaten and became a devotee again. Hiranyaksha's son Andhaka then took the kingdom and desired Uma. The text explains why Shiva was away: sages who had tricked the sage Gautama with an illusory cow were cursed by him to be outside the Veda, and Shiva and Vishnu made deluding scriptures for them (Kapala, Nakula, Vama, Bhairava, Pancharatra, Pashupata and others), through which they would pass through hell and then rise; Shiva went begging with them, leaving Parvati in Vishnu's care. Andhaka attacked Mount Mandara; Shiva as Bhairava pierced him, but Andhaka produced thousands of copies of himself, and Vishnu created a hundred goddesses who destroyed them. On returning, Shiva told the goddesses that he, Narayana and Gauri are one god, and that those who worship with a divided view go to hell. When Andhaka came again, Shiva lifted him on his trident and danced. Freed of sin, Andhaka praised Shiva, became a leader of his hosts (ganapati), praised Parvati and was taken as her son. Later the mother goddesses, hungry, began to devour the three worlds; at Bhairava's call Narasimha stopped them, and Narasimha, Bhairava and the serpent Shesha were seen as one. Vishnu taught that his dark, destroying form comes from a part of Shiva, while his form called Narayana sustains the world. The chapter ends as the story of Andhaka's killing and Bhairava's greatness.

01-017.json.summary: Kurma (Vishnu) continues the story: after Andhaka was subdued, Prahlada's son Virochana ruled justly and received the knowledge of the Self from the sage Sanatkumara, then gave the kingdom to his son Bali. Bali defeated Indra, and Aditi, the gods' mother, did penance and praised Vishnu, asking him to be born as her son; he agreed. When omens appeared in Bali's city, Prahlada told him that Vishnu had entered Aditi's womb and that he should take refuge in Vishnu, which Bali did. Aditi bore the four-armed Vishnu to Kashyapa; he received the sacred thread and learned the Vedas from Bharadvaja, showing the world the proper path. When Bali held a great sacrifice, Vishnu came as Vamana, a dwarf Brahmin student, and begged three steps of land. Bali washed his feet and poured water into his hand to seal the gift. Vishnu strode across earth, sky and heaven; his foot broke the top of the cosmic egg, and the water that poured down became the Ganga. Bali bowed and gave his own self as well. Vishnu sent him to live in Patala, enjoying pleasures even gods lack and meditating on him, promising that Bali would enter into him at the end of the age, and gave the three worlds back to Indra. In Patala, Bali learned devotion and the rules of worship from Prahlada and took refuge in Vishnu.

01-018.json.summary: Bali's eldest son, the mighty Bana, a devotee of Shiva, troubled the gods, so Shiva burned his city with one arrow. Bana came out with Shiva's linga on his head, praised him and was made a leader of his hosts. Suta then lists Kashyapa's other children: Danu's demon sons (Tara, Shambara, Svarbhanu, Vrishaparvan and others); serpents from Surasa and Kadru; gandharvas from Arishta; birds from Tamra; cows and buffaloes from Surabhi; plants from Ira; yakshas, rakshasas and apsaras from Muni and Krodhavasha. Vinata's sons were Garuda, who by penance became Vishnu's carrier through Shiva's grace, and Aruna, made the Sun's charioteer by Shiva. The children of Soma, Arishtanemi, Bahuputra, Angiras and Krishashva are named briefly. Hearing of these descendants destroys sin, and they are born again with the same names in every Manu period.

01-019.json.summary: Kashyapa's later sons, Vatsara and Asita, begin this account of the sages' lines. From them came Naidhruva, Raibhya and the great yoga teacher Devala, who gained yoga by Parvati's lord's grace. Pulastya's son Vishravas had four wives: Devavarnini bore Kubera; Kaikasi bore Ravana, Kumbhakarna, Shurpanakha and Vibhishana; Pushpotkata and Vaka bore other rakshasas such as Khara, Dushana and Trishiras. These ten rakshasas were cruel but strong in penance and devoted to Rudra. Pulaha's offspring are beasts, ghosts, snakes and elephants; Kratu had no children in this age; Bhrigu's son was Shukra, teacher of the demons and devotee of Hara. The verse on Atri's line is unclear, but it names his sons the Svastyatreyas. Narada gave Arundhati to Vasishtha and stayed childless because of Daksha's curse for misleading Daksha's sons. Vasishtha's line runs through Shakti and Parashara, who won Krishna Dvaipayana (Vyasa) by worshipping Shiva; Vyasa's son Shuka was a part of Shankara and had five ascetic sons and a daughter. Suta then turns to the royal lines.

01-020.json.summary: The solar line begins with the Sun, son of Aditi, whose wives bore Manu, Yama, Yamuna, Shani and others. Manu had nine sons, led by Ikshvaku, and a daughter Ila, who bore Pururavas to Budha and so began the lunar line. Suta follows Ikshvaku's line through many kings: Yuvanashva, who on the sage Gautama's advice worshipped Narayana for a son; Kuvalayashva, called Dhundhumara for killing the demon Dhundhu; Mandhata; and on to Vasumanas, a devotee of the Sun. After a horse sacrifice Vasumanas asked the sages which is best, sacrifice, penance or renunciation. Vasishtha advised the stages in order; most of the others said the Lord, Rudra, is worshipped by penance; Kratu said nothing but penance remains for one who has studied, sacrificed and had sons. The king gave his kingdom to his son Tridhanva and repeated the Gayatri in the Himalaya for over a hundred years. Brahma granted him another hundred years to keep repeating it, and at the end Shiva appeared in the sun's disc, three-eyed, eight-armed and half woman. Shiva told him to repeat the Shatarudriya prayer from the Yajur Veda, saying that whoever repeats it until death, living simply and devoted to ash, reaches the highest state, and gave him another hundred years. At the end of that time the king passed through yoga into the sun and on to Shiva. Reading or hearing his story frees one from sin and wins honour in Brahma's world.

01-021.json.summary: Ikshvaku's line continues with Harishchandra and King Sagara, whose wife Bhanumati chose one son, Asamanjasa, and whose wife Prabha chose sixty thousand. Sagara's descendant Bhagiratha brought down the Ganga by penance, and Shiva caught her on his head. Further down came Kalmashapada and, much later, Raghu, Aja and Dasharatha. Dasharatha's sons Rama, Bharata, Lakshmana and Shatrughna were born with Vishnu's power to destroy Ravana. Janaka had received Sita from Parvati and a bow from Shiva; Rama broke the bow and married Sita. Kaikeyi used an old boon to have her son Bharata made king, and Rama went to the forest for fourteen years with Sita and Lakshmana. Ravana, disguised as an ascetic, carried Sita off. Rama allied with Sugriva, and Hanuman found Sita in Lanka and gave her Rama's ring. Rama built a bridge across the sea, killed Ravana and his family, and recovered Sita. On the bridge he set up a linga of Shiva. Shiva appeared and promised that seeing it frees even great sinners, that bathing in the sea there removes other sins, that rites done there bear endless fruit, and that he would stay there hidden as long as the earth lasts. Rama ruled justly and worshipped Shiva with a horse sacrifice; the line ran on from his son Kusha. Hearing this line frees one from sin and wins heaven.

01-022.json.summary: Romaharshana (Suta) traces the lunar line from Pururavas through Ayu and Nahusha to Yayati. Yayati's wives Devayani and Sharmishtha bore Yadu, Turvasu, Druhyu, Anu and Puru; he made the youngest, Puru, king and gave the other sons the outer regions. Through Yadu's line came Kartavirya Arjuna, the thousand-armed king killed by Parashurama. Four of Arjuna's sons worshipped Shiva, but Jayadhvaja worshipped Vishnu, arguing that kings, born of Vishnu's part, should worship the protector. The brothers argued and asked the Seven Sages to decide. The sages said each person's chosen god is his own, and recited Brahma's list of which god suits whom: Vishnu and Indra for kings, Shiva for demons and renunciants, Brahma for celibate students, all gods for householders, and so on. So Jayadhvaja should worship Vishnu, but knowing him as one with Rudra. When the demon Videha attacked their city and broke all the brothers' weapons, Jayadhvaja remembered Vishnu; a blazing discus appeared, and he cut off the demon's head with it. Vishnu had once won this discus from Shiva. The sage Vishvamitra then taught Jayadhvaja that Narayana is the highest Self, from whom Brahma and Rudra arise, and that he must be worshipped through one's own duty without selfish desire. The brothers worshipped Rudra with sacrifices, while Vishvamitra led Jayadhvaja's sacrifice to Vishnu, at which Hari appeared in person. Hearing this story frees one from sin and leads to Vishnu's world.

01-023.json.summary: Jayadhvaja's descendants include Talajangha, Vitihotra and King Durjaya, whose story Suta tells. Durjaya, though he had a faithful wife, met the apsara Urvashi by the Yamuna and stayed with her a long time. When he returned home ashamed, his wife saw his fault by her inner sight and told him to atone, since a frightened king ruins his kingdom. The sage Kanva taught him the atonement, but on the way to the Himalaya Durjaya seized a divine garland from a gandharva and searched the world for Urvashi. He found her at Lake Manasa and stayed with her again. Fearing Kanva's curse, she urged him to leave, and when he would not, she showed him a hideous, hairy, yellow-eyed form. Disgusted with himself, he did penance for twelve years on roots and twelve more on air, then confessed to Kanva. Kanva sent him to Varanasi to bathe in the Ganga, offer water to gods and ancestors and see the Vishveshvara linga. He did so, was freed of sin, ruled again, and had a son, Supratika. A final verse about Urvashi's seven sons and daughters is unclear. Suta then turns to the line of Kroshtu.

01-024.json.summary: The line of Kroshtu, son of Yadu, is followed through many kings to Vidarbha and his sons. One descendant, Navaratha, fled from a rakshasa while hunting and took refuge at a shrine of Sarasvati, praising her as the goddess of speech, source of the worlds and Brahma's queen. A blazing being came out and killed the rakshasa, and Navaratha set up the Goddess in his city and worshipped her. A later king, Andhaka, spread the Satvata scripture on Narada's advice. Of the Yadava branches, the line of Vrishni produced Satyaki and Akrura. Another king, Anakadundubhi, won boons from Brahma at Govardhana. He worshipped Shiva with song and received from him a divine bride, and their descendants became masters of music. Ahuka's sons were Ugrasena, father of Kamsa, and Devaka, whose daughter Devaki married Vasudeva. Hari was born as Devaki's son Krishna at the gods' request, Balarama (Shesha) was born to Rohini, and Yoganidra, born from Uma, became Yashoda's daughter. Kamsa had killed Devaki's earlier sons. Krishna had sixteen thousand wives and countless sons, the best being Rukmini's sons such as Pradyumna. When Jambavati asked for an equally fine son, Krishna began penance, which the next chapter tells.

01-025.json.summary: Krishna, though he needed nothing, did penance for a son to show that Ishvara is his own root, Suta says. Riding Garuda, he came to the sage Upamanyu's hermitage by the Ganga, full of ash-smeared ascetics devoted to Shiva, who recognised him as Narayana. He bathed, offered water to gods and ancestors and worshipped the lingas along the rivers. Upamanyu welcomed him and asked why he had come. Krishna said he wished to see Shiva. Upamanyu said Shiva is seen through devotion and fierce penance, and listed sages who had won grace there: Vasishtha, Vyasa, Yajnavalkya and Bhrigu, father of Shukra. A bracketed, partly corrupt passage adds that the Vayaviya Purana was made known there. Upamanyu gave Krishna the Pashupata vow and yoga. Ash-covered, shaven and in bark clothes, Krishna repeated Rudra's prayer for a long time. At last Shiva appeared in the sky with the Goddess, blazing, armed and three-eyed, with Brahma, Krishna himself, the hosts and the great sages around him. Krishna praised him as the source of all, Brahma and Hari, adding a long string of salutations, and said even one flower offered at his feet frees a person. Shiva lifted him, called him his own highest form, Narayana, and granted him a son like himself and devoted to Shiva. The Goddess said there is no difference between them and gave him all-knowing, lordship and firm devotion. Then Shiva took Krishna by the hand to Kailasa.

01-026.json.summary: On Kailasa, Suta tells, Krishna stayed for a long time with Shiva; gandharva, apsara and naga women fell in love with him, and taking many forms he fulfilled their wishes. Meanwhile Dvaraka was afraid without him. Garuda defended the city from demons, and when Narada said where Krishna was, Garuda flew to Kailasa and brought him the news. With Shiva's leave Krishna returned, and the city welcomed him with music and flowers. When sages led by Markandeya came, Krishna honoured them, and after his midday rites he worshipped Shiva in a linga with Markandeya. Markandeya asked whom he, the highest Brahman, could be worshipping. Krishna said he worships Ishvara to show deluded people the root of his own self, and that there is no difference between them. The linga, he said, is the unmanifest, imperishable light. He told its origin: in the ocean of dissolution he and Brahma argued over who was the creator, and a fiery linga without end appeared. Brahma went up and Krishna went down for a hundred years without finding its end, and they praised Shiva with the refrain 'Salutation to Shiva, Brahman in the form of the linga'. Shiva appeared and said both were born from his body. He is one, but divided as Brahma, Vishnu and Hara for creation, protection and dissolution. He would be born from Brahma's face as the trident-bearer. From then on linga worship was established. Markandeya left, told to meditate on Hara to cross worldly life. Whoever recites, hears or reads this chapter is freed of all sins, and one who repeats it daily is honoured in Brahma's world.

01-027.json.summary: Suta tells how Krishna ends his work on earth. After a boon from Shiva, Krishna has the son Samba by Jambavati, and Pradyumna has Aniruddha. Having killed Kamsa, Naraka and many demons and defeated Indra and Bana, Krishna decides to return to his own abode. The sages led by Bhrigu come to Dvaraka, and he tells them the terrible Kali age has come. Those who remember him even once in Kali lose their sin, and those who worship him by the Vedic rule reach his state. But those who hate or blame Shiva lose the fruit of all their meditation and sacrifice and go to hell, so blame of Shiva must be avoided in deed, mind and word. Brahmins cursed by Dadhicha and Gautama will be born in Kali and must be avoided. The sages leave, and Krishna withdraws his clan and goes to the highest state. Hearing this account of the royal lines frees one from sin and brings honour in heaven.

01-028.json.summary: This very short chapter leads into the next. The sages ask Suta about the four ages. Suta tells how, after Krishna has gone, Arjuna, full of grief, performs the last rites and meets the sage Vyasa on the road with his pupils. Arjuna falls at his feet, says his grief has gone at the sight of him, and asks what he should do now. Vyasa sits down on a river bank to answer; the answer follows in the next chapter.

01-029.json.summary: Vyasa tells Arjuna that the terrible Kali age has come, when people will be sinful and abandon caste and life-stage duties, so he is going to Varanasi, the only atonement he sees for Kali. He tells Arjuna to keep his own duty. Asked about the ages, Vyasa explains: the highest practice is meditation in Krita, knowledge in Treta, sacrifice in Dvapara and giving in Kali; the chief god is Brahma, the Sun, Vishnu and Rudra in turn, though Rudra is worshipped in all four. Dharma stands on four feet in Krita and loses one in each age. In Krita people were born in pairs, equal, content, without homes and devoted to Mahadeva. In Treta that perfection was lost; "house trees" gave people clothes, fruit and honey, but greed made them vanish, and after people suffered from cold and heat, rain brought rivers and plants that grew without ploughing. Greed returned, the plants sank into the earth, and Prithu milked the earth. As people seized one another's wealth and wives, Brahma created Kshatriyas to keep order and set up the castes and life stages, with sacrifice free of animal killing. In Dvapara people's views differ; the one Veda is divided into four by the Vyasas and split further into many branches, and the histories, Puranas and law books arise. Drought, death and disease make people weary, which leads to detachment and knowledge. Dharma, full in Krita, is disturbed in Dvapara and perishes in Kali.

01-030.json.summary: Vyasa describes the Kali age to Arjuna. People are deceitful, angry, greedy and untruthful; disease, hunger and drought are common. The twice-born stop studying the Veda and doing rites, blame Shiva, Vishnu, the Vedas and the Puranas, and follow rites outside the Veda. Kings are mostly Shudras and oppress Brahmins; Shudras in ochre robes teach dharma and sit on high seats, while poorly learned Brahmins serve and praise them and teach them the Veda. False sects, sellers of the Veda and of holy places, and followers of left-hand Pashupata and Pancharatra ways appear. Brahmins once cursed by Dadhicha and Gautama are reborn and blame Mahadeva and Vishnu. Yet in Kali Rudra, as Shankara Nilalohita, will take forms to uphold Vedic duties and teach the knowledge of Brahman. Those who serve him in any way overcome Kali's faults, and gaining great merit with little effort is Kali's great virtue. So a Brahmin especially should take refuge in Rudra; bowing to him gives the fruit of all rites, unlike bowing to other gods, and without his worship gifts, penance and sacrifice are in vain. A hymn of praise to Rudra follows, naming him Tryambaka, Shambhu, Sthanu, Virupaksha, Nilakantha, Pashupati and others. Vyasa adds that this account fits all past and future ages. Arjuna becomes firmly devoted to Shiva and bows to Vyasa, who praises him as Shankara's greatest devotee, tells him to go home without grief, and leaves for Shiva's city. Arjuna gives up other rites for devotion to Shiva. Suta calls Vyasa Vishnu himself and asks the sages to bow to him, which they do.

01-031.json.summary: The sages ask what Vyasa did in Varanasi. Suta says he bathed in the Ganga and worshipped Vishveshvara, and the sages there asked him for holy teachings. Jaimini, his pupil, asks which path is best among meditation, yoga, penance, celibacy, truth, giving, pilgrimage and the rest. Vyasa tells a secret teaching, not to be given to those without faith: on Mount Meru the Goddess asked Shiva how one can see him quickly, since other paths are full of effort. Shiva answered that his city Varanasi, called Avimukta, is the most secret holy place, carrying all beings across rebirth. Whatever is given, offered or practised there becomes imperishable, and the sins of thousands of births are destroyed on entering it. People of every caste, women, foreigners, even worms and birds who die there are born in Shiva's city with three eyes and the moon on the head; no one dying there goes to hell. Knowing that liberation is rare, one should stay in Varanasi even if beaten or hindered, for it gives a state not won by gifts, penance or learning. Other famous holy places such as Prayaga, Kedara, Gaya and Pushkara do not give the release that death in Varanasi gives. Elsewhere release takes a thousand births; here it takes one. It is called Avimukta because Shiva never leaves it, and at death he himself teaches the saving mantra there. The city lies between the Varana and Asi rivers. Even the worst sinners reach the highest goal there, so a seeker should live there until death and avoid sin, though obstacles will come. Only those who worshipped Rudra in a former birth find it, and no one should turn from going there, even at the word of the Veda, parents or teacher. Vyasa then wandered in Varanasi with his pupils.

01-032.json.summary: Vyasa goes with his pupils to the Omkara linga in Varanasi and tells its greatness. Merely remembering it frees one from all sins. It is called the "five-seated" linga, holding the five-fold Pashupata knowledge and the five gods beginning with Brahma; one who remembers it reaches the supreme light at death. Vyasa names the secret lingas of Varanasi: Krittivaseshvara, Madhyameshvara, Vishveshvara, Omkara and Kapardishvara, known only by Shiva's grace. At Krittivaseshvara he tells its story: a demon in the form of an elephant came to kill the Brahmins worshipping there, and Shiva burst out of the linga, killed it with his trident and wore its hide, so he is called Krittivasa, "clothed in a hide". Sages reached the highest state here in their own bodies, and those who stay at Krittivasa in the Kali age gain release in one birth instead of a thousand. Brahmins here worship Shiva in every age and recite the Shatarudriya. The chapter ends with verses praising Shiva.

01-033.json.summary: Vyasa goes to the Kapardishvara linga, bathes at the Pishachamochana pond, offers water to the ancestors and worships Shiva. There the sages see a wonder: a tiger kills a doe that runs around the linga in fear, and at once she rises into the sky in Shiva's own form, three-eyed and riding a bull, becomes a leader of his hosts and vanishes. Vyasa explains the shrine's greatness: yogis who meditate here succeed in six months, and worship after bathing in the pond destroys sins such as killing a Brahmin. Long ago the ascetic Shankukarna lived here worshipping Shiva. A starving ghost came to him and said that in his last birth he was a rich Brahmin who never worshipped gods or fed guests, but once saw, touched and bowed to Vishveshvara in Varanasi; because of that he did not see Yama after death, but became a hungry ghost. Shankukarna told him that act was great merit and that he should bathe in the pond. The ghost bathed, remembering Shiva, died, and rose in divine form in a shining chariot, praised by gods and siddhas, and entered the sun's sphere. Shankukarna then praised Shiva with the hymn called Brahmapara, and as he fell to the ground chanting Om, a blazing linga appeared and he merged into it. Hearing this story brings nearness to Rudra, and reciting the hymn morning and noon brings the highest yoga. Vyasa stayed there with his pupils worshipping Shiva.

01-034.json.summary: After many years at Kapardishvara, Vyasa goes to Madhyameshvara, bathes in the Mandakini river and worships Shiva. Ash-smeared Pashupata ascetics arrive and ask who he is; his pupils say he is Vyasa, who divided the Vedas and is devoted to Shiva. The Pashupatas ask for Shiva's secret knowledge. Vyasa sends his pupils away and teaches them; at once a pure light appears, and they merge into it and vanish. Vyasa then tells his pupils the shrine's greatness: Shiva always lives here with the Goddess. Krishna once lived here a year among Pashupatas, keeping their vow and worshipping Shiva, and Shiva gave him a boon that Shiva's devotees who worship Govinda would gain divine knowledge and that the twice-born would honour Krishna. Those who bathe here and see Shiva lose great sins, and even sinners who die here reach the highest place. Bathing, gifts, shraddha and rice-ball offerings here purify seven generations and give ten times the fruit of bathing at Sannihati during an eclipse. Vyasa lived there a long time.

01-035.json.summary: Vyasa visits the many holy places of Varanasi with Jaimini and others. Suta names the chief ones, such as Prayaga, Kala, Gauri, Svargadvara, Gaya, Narayana, Varaha, Manikarna, Kedara, Lolarka and Kapalamochana, which destroys the sin of killing a Brahmin, and others too many to count. A bracketed passage tells that Vishnu installed a linga Brahma had brought, saying his devotion to Rudra was firmer, and named it after Brahma. At each place Vyasa bathes, worships Shiva, fasts and makes offerings to the ancestors. He then sends his pupils home and stays in Varanasi, living on alms. One day he gets no alms anywhere and, in anger, decides to curse the people there. At once the Goddess appears in human form, stops him and gives him food, but says that because he is angry and ungrateful he may not live in this holy city. Recognising her, Vyasa praises her and asks to be allowed in on the eighth and fourteenth lunar days; she agrees. So Vyasa stayed close by, and the wise live in the city. Reading or hearing this greatness of Avimukta, or reciting it at rites, leads to the highest goal.

01-036.json.summary: The sages ask Suta about Prayaga. He repeats what Markandeya told Yudhishthira. After the war, Yudhishthira is overcome by grief. Markandeya comes to Hastinapura and is warmly honoured, and Yudhishthira asks how to be freed from the sin of killing many innocent men. Markandeya says going to Prayaga is best, for Shiva and Brahma live there. It is Prajapati's famous field: those who bathe there go to heaven, and those who die there are not reborn. Brahma and the gods guard it, the Sun guards the Yamuna, Indra lives there, and Shiva guards the banyan tree. Even remembering, seeing or naming Prayaga, or touching its earth, removes sin, and one who remembers the Ganga from far away reaches the highest goal. One who dies at the meeting of Ganga and Yamuna enjoys heaven in shining chariots, and when his merit ends is born in a rich family and returns there. One who dies remembering Prayaga reaches Brahma's world. But one who accepts gifts there gains nothing from the holy place, so Brahmins should not accept gifts at tirthas. One who gives a cow with gold-covered horns and silver hooves there is honoured in Rudra's world for as many thousands of years as the cow has hairs.

01-037.json.summary: Markandeya gives the rules of pilgrimage to Prayaga. One who goes riding a bull falls into hell for ages and his ancestors refuse his offerings; one who travels by vehicle out of pride or greed loses the fruit, so vehicles should be avoided. Giving a daughter in marriage by the sages' rite at the meeting of the rivers saves one from hell. One who dies at the root of the banyan tree goes to Rudra's world. The land between Ganga and Yamuna is called the hip of the earth, and bathing at the meeting gives the fruit of the Rajasuya and horse sacrifices; no one, not even one's mother, should turn one away from going. Countless other tirthas are present here. Places named include the nagas Kambala and Ashvatara, Pratishthana, Hamsaprapatana, the sandbank of Urvashi and Kotitirtha, each with its reward in heaven. The Ganga saves beings on earth, below and in heaven, so she is "three-pathed"; as long as a man's bones lie in her, he stays in heaven. She is easy to reach everywhere but rare at Gangadvara, Prayaga and the sea. Naimisha was best in Krita, Pushkara in Treta, Kurukshetra in Dvapara and the Ganga in Kali. Whoever dies in the Ganga goes to heaven and never sees hell.

01-038.json.summary: Markandeya continues on Prayaga. In the month of Magha countless tirthas gather at the meeting of Ganga and Yamuna, and three days' bathing there then equals giving a hundred thousand cows. Those who give themselves to fire or water there, stand head down drinking a stream (the word is unclear), or give their body to the birds, enjoy heaven or the moon's world for many thousands of years and are then reborn as kings or rich men. Bathing at Rinapramochana, south of Prayaga on the Yamuna, frees one from debts and gives the Sun's world.

01-039.json.summary: Markandeya praises the Yamuna, daughter of the Sun, which joins the Ganga at Prayaga. Bathing in and drinking it frees one from sin and purifies seven generations, and dying there brings the highest goal. On its south bank are the Agni tirtha and Yama's tirtha called Anaraka ("no hell"); bathing there on the fourteenth of the dark fortnight frees one from great sins. Countless tirthas are present at Prayaga, and wherever the Ganga flows, or Shiva lives as Vateshvara, is a place of penance and perfection. This teaching should be shared with good people and pupils; one who studies or hears it becomes pure and remembers past births. Markandeya then describes other tirthas and the layout of the earth and the stars, and departs. Hearing this in the morning leads to Rudra's world.

01-040.json.summary: The sages of Naimisha ask Suta about the layout of the three worlds and the kings who ruled the earth. Suta, bowing to Vishnu, begins with Priyavrata, son of Svayambhuva Manu, who had ten sons. Three of them were yogis who did not want to rule, so Priyavrata made the other seven kings of the seven continents: Agnidhra of Jambudvipa, Medhatithi of Plaksha, Vapushman of Shalmali, Jyotishman of Kusha, Dyutiman of Krauncha, Havya of Shaka and Savana of Pushkara. Their sons in turn gave their names to the regions of each continent; in these continents, the text says, keeping one's duty by caste and life stage leads to release. Agnidhra divided Jambudvipa among his nine sons, Nabhi, Kimpurusha, Hari, Ilavrita, Ramya, Hiranvan, Kuru, Bhadrashva and Ketumala, giving the southern region Himahva to Nabhi and Ilavrita, with Meru in the middle, to Ilavrita, and then went to the forest to do penance. Nabhi's son by Marudevi was Rishabha, whose eldest of a hundred sons was Bharata; Rishabha crowned Bharata, became a forest hermit and a great Pashupata. Bharata's line is listed, through Sumati, Indradyumna, Prithu, Gaya and others down to Shatajit, whose chief son Vishvajyoti worshipped Brahma and fathered King Kshemaka. These mighty kings and their descendants ruled the earth.

01-041.json.summary: Suta describes the measure of the three worlds. The seven worlds are Bhur, Bhuvar, Svar, Mahar, Jana, Tapas and Satya. The earth reaches as far as the sun's and moon's rays, the middle space reaches to the sun, and heaven reaches up to the pole star, with the seven bands of wind. The sun is a hundred thousand yojanas above the earth; above it come the moon, the lunar mansions, Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn, then the Seven Sages and finally the pole star (Dhruva), the pivot of the wheel of lights, where Vishnu stands. Sizes are given: the sun is nine thousand yojanas across, the moon twice that, and Rahu, made from the earth's shadow, equals them; the planets are smaller fractions. Saturn, Jupiter and Mars move slowly; the sun, moon, Mercury and Venus fast. The sun's chariot has a wheel of time made of the year, with three naves, five spokes and six rims, and seven horses that are the Vedic metres, such as Gayatri and Trishtubh. On Mount Manasa stand the cities of Indra, Yama, Varuna and Soma in the four directions. The sun turns like a potter's wheel, making day and night, so that it is always midday somewhere. The three worlds have the sun as their root; the light of all gods is his. The sun is called Mahadeva and the supreme deity, the twelve Adityas are parts of him, and all beings worship him.

01-042.json.summary: Suta describes who rides on the sun's chariot. In turn, through the seasons, it carries the twelve Adityas (Dhata, Aryaman, Mitra, Varuna, Indra and others), sages such as Pulastya, Atri and Vasishtha who praise the sun with hymns, leaders who hold the reins, rakshasas who go in front, serpents such as Vasuki and Takshaka who draw it, gandharvas such as Tumburu and Narada who sing, and apsaras such as Menaka, Urvashi and Rambha who dance. These beings live in the sun two by two, two months at a time, increasing his power, while the Valakhilya sages lead him from rising to setting. Together they heat, rain, shine and create, remove the bad deeds of beings and protect all creatures. The sun shines according to their strength, makes day and night, and feeds ancestors, gods and men. In the sun shines Mahadeva himself, and knowers of the Veda say the sun is his seat.

01-043.json.summary: Suta explains that Shiva in the form of the sun rules time. Of the sun's rays, seven are chief and feed the planets: Sushumna feeds the moon, and others feed Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn (the line for one ray is missing). The sun draws up water through a thousand channels and gives back rain, cold and heat: four hundred rays bring rain, three hundred cold and three hundred heat. With these he feeds men with plants, ancestors with svadha and gods with nectar. A different sun rules each month, such as Varuna in Magha, Indra in Jyeshtha and Vishnu in Pausha, each with a set number of thousands of rays, and the sun's colour changes with the seasons. The other eight planets, including Rahu and Ketu, are tied to the pole star by cords of wind and whirl after the sun, driven by the wind Pravaha. The moon's chariot has three wheels and ten white horses. In the bright fortnight the sun fills the moon with the ray Sushumna; the gods drink its nectar for half a month, and the ancestors drink the last of it at the new moon, which satisfies them for a month. So the moon is not destroyed, and its waxing and waning come from the sun. The chariots of the other planets are described with their horses. All planets and stars are bound to the pole star and turn as it turns them.

01-044.json.summary: Suta describes the higher and lower worlds. Above the pole star lie Maharloka, Janaloka (home of Sanaka and Brahma's other sons), Tapoloka and Satyaloka, Brahma's world, where there is no further death and calm yogis and ascetics enter. In Brahma's city is Narayana's palace, Vishnu's world, from which there is no return, reached by those who take refuge in him. Above it is a shining city ringed by fire, Rudra's world, where Shiva lives with the Goddess and his hosts, reached by calm, truthful Brahmins devoted to him. Below the earth are the seven netherworlds, beginning with Mahatala, adorned with jewels and palaces, where Ananta, Muchukunda and King Bali live; others are home to Vasuki, Takshaka, Prahlada, Namuchi and other nagas and demons. Below them are the hells where sinners suffer. Beneath all lies Shesha, Vishnu in serpent form, also called Kalagni Rudra, who holds up the world; at the end of time, Time rises from his mouth in poisonous flames and destroys the world. This is Shiva's dark (tamasic) form, the destroyer.

01-045.json.summary: Suta now describes the earth. Its seven continents, Jambudvipa, Plaksha, Shalmali, Kusha, Krauncha, Shaka and Pushkara, are each surrounded by an ocean, of salt water, sugarcane juice, wine, ghee, curd, milk and sweet water, each larger than the last. Jambudvipa is in the middle, and in its centre stands golden Mount Meru, eighty-four thousand yojanas high, like the seed-cup of the earth's lotus. South of it are the mountains Himavan, Hemakuta and Nishadha, and north of it Nila, Shveta and Shringi. The regions are Bharata, Kimpurusha and Harivarsha to the south, Ramyaka, Hiranmaya and the Northern Kurus to the north, and Ilavrita with Meru in the middle. Around Meru stand four buttress mountains, Mandara, Gandhamadana, Vipula and Suparshva, bearing great trees. The jambu tree gives the continent its name; its huge fruits burst on the mountain and form the Jambu river, whose drinkers know no sweat, old age or decay, and whose mud becomes the gold called jambunada. Four forests and four lakes of the gods lie around Meru, and long lists of surrounding mountains follow, such as Trikuta, Kailasa, Himavan, Anjana and Parijata, visited by gods, gandharvas and siddhas. In the valleys between them live calm sages free of sorrow.

01-046.json.summary: Suta describes the cities on and around Mount Meru. On top is Brahma's great city, where Brahma sits in yoga, worshipped by sages, Vishnu and Shiva, with Sanatkumara attending. In front of it is Shiva's shining temple, where he lives with the Goddess and accepts the worship of calm sages. Around the mountain are the cities of the guardians of the directions: Indra's Amaravati in the east, for righteous men who sacrifice; Agni's Tejovati, for those who make fire offerings; Yama's Samyamani in the south, for truthful doers of good; Nirriti's Rakshovati, ringed with rakshasas; Varuna's Shuddhavati in the west; Vayu's Gandhavati, for those devoted to breath control; Soma's Kantimati in the north, for those who keep their duty while enjoying pleasures; and Shiva's Yashovati in the north-east, which he made for his devotees. The Ganga flows from Vishnu's foot, floods the moon, falls around Brahma's city and divides into four rivers: the Sita flows east, the Alakananda south through Bharata, the Suchakshu west and the Bhadra north, each to the sea. Bharata, Ketumala, Bhadrashva and Kuru are the petals of the world lotus, and eight boundary mountains, such as Jathara, Devakuta, Kailasa and Pariyatra, stand two on each side of Meru.

01-047.json.summary: Suta describes the people of the nine regions of Jambudvipa. In Ketumala they are dark, eat jackfruit and live ten thousand years; in Bhadrashva they are white and eat mangoes; in Ramyaka and Hiranmaya they shine like silver and gold and live even longer. In the land of the Kurus people drink milk, are born in pairs and worship Shiva. In Kimpurusha people are golden and worship four-faced Brahma. In Harivarsha they drink sugarcane juice and worship Narayana, whose shining crystal palace stands there with walls, golden pillars and jewels, full of devotees and yogis. In Ilavrita people eat jambu fruit and live thirteen thousand years. In Bharata people are of many colours, worship many gods, do many kinds of work and live at most a hundred years; it is the land of action (karma-bhumi). Its seven main mountain ranges are Mahendra, Malaya, Sahya, Shuktiman, Riksha, Vindhya and Pariyatra. Bharata has nine parts; this one, surrounded by sea, has Kiratas in the east, Yavanas in the west and the four castes in the middle. Holy rivers are listed by the mountains they come from, such as the Yamuna, Sarayu and Shatadru from the Himalaya, the Narmada from Riksha, the Tapi from Vindhya, the Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri from Sahya, and the Tamraparni from Malaya, and many others; all remove sin. The peoples who drink them are named, such as the Kurus, Panchalas, Magadhas, Kalingas, Andhras and Hunas. The four ages exist only in Bharata; in the other eight regions there is no grief, hunger or fear, and people stay young.

01-048.json.summary: Suta describes the homes of gods and sages on the mountains of Jambudvipa. On Hemakuta is Shiva's crystal palace, where gods and siddhas worship him and the Goddess. On Kailasa, home of Kubera and the yakshas, is another great temple of Shiva beside the divine Mandakini river. On Sitanta are Indra's palace and Vishnu's palace, where Narayana lives with Lakshmi. Other peaks hold the homes of the Vasus, the hermitages of the Seven Sages, and a golden seat of Brahma. On Ekashringa is the hermitage of the sage Jaigishavya, who lives there with his calm, ash-smeared pupils devoted to yoga, and Shiva often comes near for their sake. Indra and Shachi live on Sumegha; the goddess Durga lives on Gajashaila, served by her many powers; rakshasas and yakshas have cities on other peaks; Garuda lives on Shvetodara meditating on Vishnu; and Lakshmi lives on Shrishringa in a golden palace. On Pariyatra is the city of Mahalakshmi, three-eyed and holding a trident, full of music and dancing apsaras. Other mountains hold the cities of Sarasvati, the gandharvas, the apsaras such as Rambha, the Rudras, Nandishvara, the Sun and the Moon, a palace where Brahma lives with Savitri, a city of siddhas such as Sanandana, cities of the danavas, and the hermitages of Kardama and Sanatkumara. Countless lakes, rivers, temples, lingas and hermitages cover these mountains; Suta says Jambudvipa could not be described in full even in hundreds of years.

01-049.json.summary: Suta describes the outer continents. Plakshadvipa, twice the size of Jambudvipa, is said here to surround the milk ocean. It has seven mountains and seven rivers; its people are free of disease and sin, there is no cycle of ages, they live five thousand years, and they worship Soma and gain union with him. Shalmali surrounds the sugarcane-juice ocean; its people, free of greed and anger, worship Vayu, and there Brahmins are tawny, kings red, Vaishyas yellow and Shudras black. Kushadvipa surrounds the wine ocean; its wise, kind people worship Brahma with sacrifices and gain union with him. Krauncha surrounds the ghee ocean; its people worship Mahadeva with sacrifice, gifts, vows and fasts and gain nearness to Rudra. Shaka surrounds the curd ocean; its people, free of disease and grief, worship the Sun and gain union with him. Each continent has its own seven mountains, rivers and four classes, all named. Beyond Shaka lies the milk ocean with Shvetadvipa, the White Island, where white-skinned people devoted to Narayana live free of illness, old age and death. Some meditate, some recite or do penance, and great devotees see the supreme Brahman called Vishnu; they have four arms and hold conch, discus and mace, while others, devoted to Shiva, wear the three lines of ash. There stands Narayana's city, with golden walls, crystal halls, gardens, music and countless lovely dancing women, which enemies of the gods cannot enter. In its centre Hari lies on the serpent Shesha, with Lakshmi holding his feet, meditated on by yogis such as Sanandana. This is Vaikuntha, where the unrighteous and those devoted to other gods do not go. From Narayana the world is born, in him it rests, and to him it returns at the end of the kalpa. The colophon of this chapter calls it the forty-eighth chapter.

01-050.json.summary: Suta completes the description of the earth. Pushkaradvipa, twice the size of Shaka, has only one mountain, Manasottara, which divides it into two regions, Mahavita and Dhatakikhanda, and it is surrounded by the sweet-water ocean. A great banyan grows there where Brahma lives, and there too Shiva, half Hara and half Hari, is worshipped by Brahma and the yogis. Its people are free of disease, grief and hatred; there is no truth or falsehood, no high or low, no caste duties, and no rivers or mountains. Beyond the ocean is a golden land, then the mountain Lokaloka, lit on one side and dark on the other, and beyond it darkness and the shell of the cosmic egg. There are thousands of millions of such eggs, each with fourteen worlds and its own Brahma, Rudras and Narayana, surrounded by seven coverings. Beyond them is endless, unmanifest Prakriti, called Brahman and the highest state. Maheshvara is beyond the unmanifest; from it comes the egg, from the egg Brahma, and by him the world is created.

01-051.json.summary: The sages ask Suta about past and future Manvantaras, the Vyasas of each Dvapara age, Shiva's forms in the Kali age and his pupils. Suta names the past Manus, Svayambhuva, Svarochisha, Uttama, Tamasa, Raivata and Chakshusha, and the present seventh, Vaivasvata, son of the Sun. For each age he gives its gods, its Indra and its Seven Sages; for example, in Svarochisha's age Indra was Vipashchit, in Tamasa's Indra was Shibi, a devotee of Shankara, and in the present age the gods are the Adityas, Vasus, Rudras and Maruts, Indra is Purandara, and the sages are Vasishtha, Kashyapa, Atri, Jamadagni, Gautama, Vishvamitra and Bharadvaja. Four of these Manus were of Priyavrata's line. Vishnu's power, full of goodness, upholds the world, and in each age he was born: as Yajna in Svayambhuva's age, then as Tushita, Satya, Hari, Manasa and Vaikuntha, and in the present age as Vamana, son of Kashyapa and Aditi, who won the three worlds in three strides and gave them to Indra. He is called Vishnu because he pervades everything, and Narayana as the inner self of beings. He stands in four forms: Vasudeva, pure knowledge beyond qualities; Time, the dark form called Shiva, which destroys all at the end; Pradyumna, who upholds and deludes the world and is called Prakriti; and Aniruddha, called Brahma, the creator. Knowing all this as Vasudeva brings release. Vyasa, who divided the Veda into four, is Narayana himself, and only he knows the supreme Brahman. Suta says this greatness of Vishnu is true, and one who knows it is not deluded. The other questions are not answered in this chapter.

01-052.json.summary: Suta tells the sages the line of Vyasas, the arrangers of the Veda, one for each Dvapara age of the present Manu period. At Brahma's command the Veda was divided again and again: the first Vyasa was Svayambhuva Manu, followed by Prajapati, Ushana, Brihaspati, Savita, Mrityu, Indra, Vasishtha, Sarasvata, Tridhama, Rishabha and others, down to Bharadvaja, Gautama, Trinabindu, Valmiki and Jatukarna in the twenty-seventh (the list skips some numbers). In the present, twenty-eighth Dvapara, the Vyasa is Krishna Dvaipayana, son of Parashara, a form of Hari, who worshipped Shiva and divided the Vedas by his grace. He took four disciples: Paila for the Rig Veda, Vaishampayana for the Yajur Veda, Jaimini for the Sama Veda and Sumantu for the Atharva Veda, with Suta himself as the fifth, to tell the histories and Puranas. The once-single Yajur Veda he divided into four, giving the sacrifice its four kinds of priests: the adhvaryu with the Yajus, the hotri with the Rik verses, the udgatri with the Saman chants and the brahman priest with the Atharva. He made the Rig Veda in twenty-one branches, the Yajur Veda in a hundred, the Sama Veda in a thousand and the Atharva in nine, and arranged the Purana in eighteen. This four-part Veda was born from Brahma as the syllable Om, which cleanses every fault. The Veda sings of the eternal Vasudeva, the highest Brahman, light and bliss; Maheshvara is himself the Veda and what it makes known, and by resting in him one is freed. The son of Parashara knows this imperishable Om and what lies beyond the Veda.

01-053.json.summary: Suta now tells the sages the incarnations of Mahadeva (Shiva) in the Kali ages of the present Vaivasvata Manu period. In the first Kali age the radiant Shveta appeared on a peak of the Himalaya for the good of Brahmins, with four disciples, Shveta, Shvetashikha, Shvetasya and Shvetalohita. The later incarnations follow in order, among them Subhava, Damana, Suhotra, Lokakshi, the yogi Jaigishavya, Dadhivaha, Rishabha, Bhrigu, Ugra, Atri, Gautama, Gokarna, Guhavasa, Shikhandi, Attahasa, Daruka, Langali, Shuli, Dindi, Mundi, Sahishnu, Somasharma, and last Nakulisha, who appears at the end of the Kali age at a holy place called Karyavatara. These are the twenty-eight incarnations of the trident-bearer. Each had four calm, devoted disciples, and Suta names them in a long list that includes Sanaka, Sanatana and Sanandana, Kapila, Asuri, Panchashikha, Parashara, Garga, Vasishtha, Atri, Ushana, Chyavana, Brihaspati, Vamadeva, Shvetaketu, Devala, Ashvalayana, Akshapada, Kushika and Ruru. These pure yogis are born at the command of the masters of yoga to establish the Veda, and Brahmins who remember, honour and offer water to them gain knowledge of Brahman. Suta then names the coming Manus: Savarna, Daksha-Savarna, Brahma-Savarna, Dharma, Rudra-Savarna, Rochamana and Bhautya. This closes the first part of the Purana, as told by Narayana. Whoever reads or hears it, or recites it to good Brahmins, is freed of all sins and rejoices with Brahma; it should be read after bathing, in a temple or on a river bank. The part ends with a salutation to Vishnu, the ancient Person, in the form of the tortoise (Kurma).

02-001.json.summary: The second part (Uttara Bhaga) opens with the Ishvara Gita. The sages ask Suta for the knowledge of Brahman that ends all the sorrow of worldly life. Just then Vyasa himself arrives; the sages honour him, Suta falls at his teacher's feet, and Suta asks him to give the sages the liberating knowledge once told by Vishnu as Kurma. Vyasa says he will tell what Mahadeva himself taught. Long ago Sanatkumara, Sanaka, Sanandana, Angiras, Bhrigu, Kapila, Vamadeva, Vasishtha and other sages, troubled by doubts, did hard penance at the Badari hermitage. There they saw the sage Narayana with Nara and asked him: what is the cause of all this, who wanders in rebirth, what is the self, what is liberation, and what is the highest Brahman? Narayana dropped his ascetic form and shone in his own glory with conch, discus and mace, and then Mahadeva appeared, the moon on his head. The sages praised Shiva as lord of beings, creator, protector and destroyer of the world. Shiva embraced Vishnu and asked why the sages had come. Vishnu said they were pure ascetics seeking true sight, and asked Shiva, who alone knows his own self, to teach them in his presence. A shining seat came down from the sky; Shiva sat on it with Vishnu, filling the world with light, and the sages saw him as the calm Lord whom yogis see within, the source and end of all beings. Shiva agreed to speak and told them to listen calmly.

02-002.json.summary: Ishvara (Shiva) begins his teaching with a secret knowledge of the self that even the gods do not grasp. The self is single, pure, subtle and eternal, pure consciousness within all; the world comes from it and dissolves in it, and though, as wielder of maya (the power of illusion), it seems to take many bodies, it does not itself wander in rebirth. It is not the elements, the senses, the mind, the doer or the enjoyer. The world and the self are as different as light and darkness. Thoughts like 'I am the doer, happy or sad, thin or fat' come from the ego and are wrongly laid on the self, which is only the witness. So worldly life rests on ignorance: joined with primal nature, the self takes the not-self for itself, and from this come attachment, hatred and deeds that cause new bodies. The self is one and seems divided only through maya, as a clear crystal looks red beside a red flower or the sky seems stained by smoke. The signs of freedom are given: seeing all beings in the self and the self in all, losing all desires, and seeing the world as only maya; as rivers merge in the sea, the self merges in the imperishable. This is Samkhya, the essence of Vedanta, and Yoga is the one-pointed mind; one who sees the two as one knows the truth, while yogis attached to powers sink. Shiva then speaks of himself as that self, who sees without eyes and hears without ears, knows all and is known by none, beyond maya yet moving all things. Yogis who enter him gain union with him, master maya and never return. This teaching should be given to sons, disciples and yogis.

02-003.json.summary: Shiva goes on to explain how the world arises. From the unmanifest came time, primal nature (pradhana) and the supreme Person, and from them all things were born, so the world is made of Brahman. That Brahman has hands, feet and eyes everywhere, yet no senses; it is the support of all, without second, beyond proof, the highest sky, and the wise call it knowledge. Shiva says he is that all-pervading Lord, and all beings rest in him. Nature, the Person and time are without beginning or end and rest in the unmanifest. Nature, which deludes all beings, brings forth the world from the Great principle (mahat) down to the gross elements; the Person dwelling in nature and enjoying its qualities is the twenty-fifth principle. From mahat rises the ego, also called the individual soul (jiva), through which one feels joy and sorrow in each birth; worldly life comes from the Person's contact with nature over time. Time creates and destroys all and is ruled by none. An order of higher principles is given: the senses, then mind, ego, mahat, the unmanifest, the Person, breath (prana), sky, and beyond the sky the fire that is the Lord. Shiva declares he is that imperishable Brahman; nothing is higher than him, and knowing him one is freed. Joined with time he creates and destroys the world, as the Veda teaches.

02-004.json.summary: Shiva now tells the greatness of the God of gods. He cannot be known by penance, gifts or sacrifice, only by the highest devotion (bhakti). He dwells in all as the witness, yet gods, sages and Brahma do not see him; the Vedas sing of him, and he enjoys all offerings and gives their fruits. To Brahmins, Kshatriyas and Vaishyas who follow dharma and worship him he gives the highest place, and those of low birth such as Shudras who keep their duty and are devoted are also freed in time. His devotees never perish; whoever scorns them scorns him, and whoever offers him even a leaf, flower, fruit or water is dear to him. He made Brahma and gave him the Vedas, teaches yogis, protects the righteous and destroys those who hate the Veda. He works through three powers: one takes Brahma's form and creates, a second becomes Narayana and preserves, and a third, dark power called time, in Rudra's form, destroys.
