Maya is his power that deludes the world, and knowledge is his higher power, by which he destroys maya in yogis' hearts. Some reach him by meditation, some by knowledge, some by devotion or action; dearest is the one who worships him through knowledge, but devotees of Hari also reach him and do not return. Resting in bliss, he moves the world and dances forever as the yogi; whoever knows this knows the Veda. This secret is to be given only to the calm and righteous who keep the sacred fires.

02-005.json.summary: Vyasa tells how Shiva, having said this much, began to dance, showing his highest divine state. The sages saw him dancing in the clear sky with Vishnu: with a thousand heads, arms and feet, matted hair crowned with the crescent moon, wearing a tiger skin, holding a trident, with sun, moon and fire as his three eyes, fearsome with fangs, bright as millions of suns, filling the cosmic egg inside and out, sending out flames and burning the whole world. In a moment they saw Narayana become one with him, and seeing this form of Rudra and Narayana together they felt their lives fulfilled. Sanatkumara, Bhrigu, Angiras, Kapila, Marichi and the others bowed, uttered Om and praised him in a long hymn: he is the one Lord dwelling in the heart, smaller than the smallest and greater than the greatest; Hiranyagarbha and the Vedas came from him; he turns the wheel of Brahman as master of maya; Om is his name and the seed of freedom; he is Rudra, Brahma, Vishnu, Agni, Indra and the Sun; lasting peace belongs only to those who take refuge in him, and remembering his feet destroys the seed of rebirth. They ended with salutations to Bhava, Hara, Rudra and Shiva. Pleased, Shiva withdrew his great form. The amazed sages said the vision had given them peace and unwavering devotion, and asked to hear more of his greatness. Looking at Vishnu, Shiva began to reply.

02-006.json.summary: In answer, Shiva explains that he alone makes, guards and destroys the worlds; all rests in him, yet he is not contained in all. The wonderful form they saw was only a likeness shown by his maya. As time he drives the world; at the start of creation he stirs primal nature and the Person, and from their union the world unfolds. Hiranyagarbha, born from his body, received from him divine power and the four Vedas, and as four-faced Brahma creates by his order; Narayana, his highest form, protects; and Rudra, who is time, destroys at his command. He then lists the powers that act only by his order: Agni carries offerings and digests food in the body, Varuna gives life through the waters, the wind holds up bodies, Soma nourishes, the sun gives light and rain, Indra rules and rewards sacrificers, Yama punishes the wicked, Kubera gives wealth, Nirriti rules the Rakshasas, Vinayaka makes obstacles, Skanda leads the gods' army, Shri gives fortune, Sarasvati speech, Savitri saves men from hell, Parvati gives the knowledge of Brahman, Shesha holds the world on his head, and the fourteen Manus guard all people. All other gods and beings, all divisions of time, all worlds and cosmic eggs past and future, the elements, maya itself, the Person in every body and the very intellect that sees truth act under his command. In short, the world is made of his power and dissolves in him; he is the highest Brahman, and nothing exists apart from him. Knowing this frees a being from the bonds of rebirth.

02-007.json.summary: Continuing, Shiva describes his power, knowing which a person is freed. His highest home is the eternal, partless, blissful Brahman. He names himself as the best in each class: among yogis Shambhu, among women the mountain's daughter, among Adityas Vishnu, among birds Garuda, among seers Vasishtha, among sages Vyasa, among mountains Meru, among vows truth, among stages of life the householder, among Vedas the Sama Veda, among recitations the Gayatri, among secrets Om, among holy places Avimukta (Varanasi), among kinds of knowledge the knowledge of the self, among bonds maya, among goals liberation; whatever is mighty and bright is a spark of his glory. All selves caught in worldly life are pashus (bound creatures, literally cattle), and he is their lord, Pashupati; he binds them in play with the noose of maya, and he alone frees them. The bonds are the twenty-four principles (the eight natures, ten organs, five objects and the unmanifest primal nature), maya, karma and the qualities, together with the afflictions. Nature is the balance of the three qualities: sattva (knowledge), tamas (ignorance) and rajas (a mix of both). The two bonds of karma are merit and sin, but actions offered to him do not bind. The five afflictions are ignorance, egoism, attachment, hatred and clinging to life, and their cause is maya, a power resting in him. He is himself the bond, the binder and the keeper of the bound; he knows all and none knows him.

02-008.json.summary: Shiva gives another secret teaching by which a being crosses the ocean of worldly life. The great Brahman is his womb, and in it he places the seed called root maya, from which the world is born: primal nature, the Person, mahat, the elements and the senses. Then came a golden egg as bright as millions of suns, in which the great Brahma was born through his power. All living beings are made of him, but, deluded by maya, they do not see him as their father; one who knows him as the seed-giving father is never deluded. Whoever sees the Lord dwelling equally in all beings, undying among the dying, truly sees, does no harm to the self and reaches the highest goal. One who knows the seven subtle things (the five subtle elements, mind and self), the six limbs of the Lord (all-knowing, contentment, beginningless awareness, freedom, unfailing power and endless power) and the working of primal nature reaches the highest Brahman. The power hidden in nature, called in the Vedas the womb of Brahman, has one ruler: Maheshvara, the true Person, the one Rudra, the seed and the universe. Some call him one, some many; the Veda-knowers call him smaller than the smallest and greater than the greatest. Whoever knows this golden, all-formed Person hidden in the heart goes beyond the intellect and stands firm.

02-009.json.summary: The sages ask Mahadeva how he, partless, pure and actionless, can be the form of the universe. He answers that he is not the universe, yet nothing exists apart from him. The cause is maya, a beginningless and endless power resting in him, through which the spread-out world came from the unmanifest. The unmanifest cause is bliss, light and the imperishable, and he himself is that highest Brahman; this is why the Brahman-knowers call him the universe in form, explaining how he is both one and many, while no fault touches the self. Through his many powers the eternal Brahman only seems different: by one comes union with him, by another the outward life of the soul, which seems to act only through ignorance. That shining imperishable light is the highest place of Vishnu, in which the whole world is woven; knowing it, one is freed. Words and mind turn back from it without reaching it, and one who knows the bliss of Brahman fears nothing. Knowing the great Person, sun-coloured and beyond darkness, the wise become Brahman, full of bliss, and go where there is no return. The one God hidden in all beings, the inner self of all, gives lasting peace to the wise who see him, and to no others. This divine knowledge should be kept secret; it is hard to gain even for yogis.

02-010.json.summary: The Lord now explains that the one unmanifest, which has no marks (alinga), is the true mark (linga) called Brahman: the self-shining highest reality in the highest sky, beyond qualities, pure knowledge. The wise, desires stilled and minds fixed on it, see that highest Brahman, which the Veda calls the linga; there is no other way to see him, and all other knowledge is ignorance, since the world is made of maya. Even those who see many forms reach the Highest if they hold firm devotion, and those who see the Lord with devotion, as one or many, become one with him. They see the supreme Lord directly as their own self, eternal bliss and truth. This is the highest liberation, called union (sayujya), nirvana, oneness with Brahman and aloneness (kaivalya). The one Shiva, without beginning, middle or end, is Mahadeva, and knowing him one is freed. There the sun, moon, stars and lightning do not shine; by his light all shines. The Vedas call him eternal bliss and truth, and the wise meditate on him with Om. In the highest sky there is no earth, water, fire, wind, mind or intellect; only Shiva shines. The yogi who knows this secret should practise yoga always, with effort, in a lonely place.

02-011.json.summary: In the last chapter of the Ishvara Gita, Shiva teaches the sages the yoga by which one sees the Lord as one's own self. The fire of yoga burns up all sin, and yoga and knowledge feed each other. Yoga is of two kinds: the yoga of absence (abhava), meditating on one's nature as empty, and the great yoga, seeing the self as eternal bliss and one with him, which far surpasses all others. Its eight limbs are explained: the restraints (non-violence, truth, not stealing, celibacy, owning nothing), the observances (penance, study and recitation, contentment, purity, devotion to Shiva), breath control, withdrawal of the senses, fixing the mind, meditation and absorption (samadhi), with the lotus and other postures. Yoga is done in a clean, quiet place such as a cave, river bank or temple, not near fire, cremation grounds or crowds. The yogi bows to the masters, Vinayaka, the guru and Shiva, sits with eyes on the nose tip, and meditates on a lotus above the head or in the heart holding the imperishable light named by Om, placing his self in it; he may also smear himself with sacred ash. This is the Pashupata yoga, which frees the bound soul, meant for devoted twice-born celibates who keep vows of celibacy, non-violence, patience, truth and the like. Shiva describes the devotee he loves, free of ego, fear and anger, giving him the fruits of all acts. One should take refuge in him alone and worship the linga until death: yogis in the heart, others in fire, water, the sun or images. One not yet wise should repeat Om or the Shatarudriya, or live in Varanasi, where Shiva gives every dying being freeing knowledge. Vyasa then tells how Shiva declared that Narayana is himself: those who see the two as one are freed, those who see a difference go to hell. Shiva and Narayana vanished, telling the sages to pass the knowledge on. Vyasa traces the teachers, such as Sanatkumara to Samvarta and he to Satyavrata, and says he received it from Vamadeva-Rudra. The sages then ask him for the yoga of action. Reading or hearing this dialogue frees one from all sins and leads to Brahma's world.

02-012.json.summary: Vyasa begins the yoga of action (karma yoga) for Brahmins, as Manu taught it. After the sacred-thread ceremony in the eighth year, the boy studies the Vedas, carrying staff and girdle, wearing the thread and a black antelope skin, living on alms and serving his teacher. The thread is always worn and the tuft tied, or rites are void; it hangs over the left shoulder normally, round the neck at some times, and over the right shoulder for rites to the ancestors. He worships at both twilights, since one who drops this becomes an outcaste, tends the fire and offers water to gods, seers and ancestors. He greets elders by saying his own name, and they bless him with 'Live long'. His elders (gurus) include parents, teacher, elder brother, king, uncles and grandparents; he must rise for them and never argue with them. Father, mother, teacher, elder brother and master are honoured most, the mother above all; while his parents live he does no other dharma without their leave, for there is no god like the mother and no guru like the father. A Brahmin is greeted by the other castes but only blesses them in return. Fire is the guru of the twice-born, the Brahmin of all castes, the husband of women, and the guest of everyone. Learning, deeds, age, kinship and wealth earn respect, in that order, and even a Shudra over ninety deserves it; way is made for Brahmins, women, kings, the old, the sick and others. The student begs daily from good homes, first from his mother or aunts, gives the food to his teacher and eats it silently with his leave; living on alms counts as fasting. He honours his food, avoids overeating, eats facing east, and sips water before and after.

02-013.json.summary: Vyasa gives the rules for sipping water (achamana) and bodily purity. A twice-born sips water again after eating, sleeping, bathing, walking in the street, passing urine or stool, spitting, coughing, starting study, visiting a cremation ground, at the twilights, after speaking with Chandalas, Shudras or the impure, and after tears or bleeding, among others. He sips seated, facing east or north, with pure, cool water, not standing, talking, laughing or with shoes on. A Brahmin is purified when the water reaches his heart, a Kshatriya his throat, a Vaishya when it is drunk, and women and Shudras by a touch at the lips. The hand has holy spots: Brahma's at the base of the thumb, the ancestors' between thumb and forefinger, the gods' at the fingertips and others; one sips with Brahma's spot. He sips three times, then touches mouth, eyes, nostrils, ears, heart and head, which pleases Brahma, Vishnu, Shiva and other gods in turn. Drops falling on the body do not defile, and Manu sees no fault in betel, fruit or sugarcane. To relieve himself he puts the sacred thread over the right ear, faces north by day and south by night, and covers the ground and his head, never doing so in shade, water, a road, a field, a temple, a cremation ground or similar places, nor facing the sun, fire, cows, Brahmins or women. He then cleans himself with earth from a river bank and water until all smell and stain are gone, and sips water by the rules.

02-014.json.summary: Vyasa continues with the conduct of the Vedic student. He studies when called, sits facing his teacher, never speaks his bare name, mimics him or answers him lying or eating, leaves when the teacher is blamed, fetches water, kusha and firewood, and never steps on his seat, sandals or shadow. He controls his senses and avoids perfumes, garlands, music, dancing, gossip, sleep, and looking at or touching women, among other things. He must never abandon his teacher, though Manu allows leaving one who has gone astray. The teacher's wife is honoured like him, but a young one is greeted on the ground, not at her feet. A teacher who keeps a pupil a year without teaching takes on his sins. Study begins with sipping water, touching the teacher's feet, breath control and Om. The Veda is the eternal eye of all beings, and a Brahmin who does not study it falls from Brahminhood; study of the four Vedas pleases the gods like offerings of milk, curd, ghee and honey, and study of the Puranas like offerings of meat. He recites the Gayatri daily, ten, a hundred or a thousand times, with Om and the three great vyahritis; nothing is higher to recite. Yearly study starts on the full moon of Shravana or nearby months, lasts four and a half months, and then the Vedas are studied in bright fortnights and the Puranas in dark ones. Study stops at set times, such as storms, eclipses, a corpse or a Shudra nearby, the new and full moon, and after a teacher's death, because Rakshasas strike then; daily rites have no break. One who recites without understanding sinks like a cow in mud. A student may serve his teacher for life or live in the forest reciting sacred texts. Following this rule with the heart given to the Lord leads to Shiva's state.

02-015.json.summary: Vyasa describes the householder. After learning the Vedas and paying his teacher, the twice-born takes the graduation bath. The graduate wears white, two sacred threads and gold earrings, carries a staff, water pot and umbrella, and keeps hair and nails trimmed. He should marry a good wife of his own kind, not of his mother's gotra or his own seer-line, and approach her in her fertile season, avoiding certain lunar days. He keeps the household fire, does his Vedic duties (failing which he falls into terrible hells), performs the five great sacrifices and twilight worship, and supports his wife. He should not boast of good deeds or hide sins, should be kind to all, suit his dress and speech to his age, wealth and learning, and follow the path of his forefathers. Truthful, free of anger and envy, devoted to his parents, cows and Brahmins, he is honoured in Brahma's world; one who shares, is patient and kind is a true householder, not merely one with a house. The marks of a Brahmin are patience (bearing harm), kindness (feeling others' pain as one's own), knowledge, truth (saying things as they are), self-control, calm, and devotion to the inner self; true knowledge is that by which Mahadeva is known. The body must be guarded as the home of dharma. He pursues dharma, wealth and pleasure but never against dharma, does no wrong even when suffering, and never reviles the Vedas or gods. A Brahmin who reads or teaches this chapter is honoured in Brahma's world.

02-016.json.summary: Vyasa lists rules of conduct for a twice-born. He must harm no being, never lie or steal, for taking even another's grass or water leads to hell, and never take what belongs to gods or Brahmins, which is the real poison. He should not accept gifts from a king, a Shudra or an outcaste, hide sins behind vows, or live by wearing the marks of an order he does not belong to. He must not honour heretics, followers of the left-hand path, Pancharatras or Pashupatas, nor keep company with those who revile the Vedas, gods or Brahmins. Betraying the guru is far worse than offending the gods. Families decline through bad marriages, neglect of rites, lying and forbidden food. He should live in the land between the Himalaya and the Vindhya, where the black antelope roams, not in a kingdom ruled by Shudras or among heretics. Eleven kinds of contact, such as sharing a seat, food or marriage, cause 'mixing', so he must avoid them. He avoids quarrels and gossip, does not do to others what he dislikes, and leaves when gods or Vedas are reviled, for revilers have no atonement. False accusation is worse than the great sins. A long list of prohibitions follows, for example not looking at the rising sun or a naked person, not eating with his wife, not teaching dharma to a Shudra, not bathing naked, not gambling, dancing or learning a foreign tongue, not stretching his feet towards gods or fire, and not performing rites while impure. The text both forbids blowing on fire with the mouth and later says fire should be blown only with the mouth. He should not speak to another's wife or travel alone or at night, and must avoid forbidden food and drink.

02-017.json.summary: Vyasa tells whose food may be eaten and what is forbidden. A Brahmin who eats a Shudra's food when not in distress goes to a Shudra's womb, and one who eats it for six months becomes a Shudra in life and a dog after death. He refuses the food of a king, dancer, courtesan, thief, liquor-seller, physician, moneylender, atheist and many others, and food given with contempt, since whoever eats someone's food eats his sins. From some Shudras, such as one's cowherd, barber or farm worker, food may be taken. Forbidden foods include onion, garlic, mushrooms, village pig, certain fruits and greens, stale or recooked food, and food touched by a dog, a Chandala or a menstruating woman. Manu forbids the milk of a cow without a calf, of a camel and of a sheep. Most birds and beasts are forbidden, such as the parrot, owl, village cock, lion, dog and monkey, but a few, such as the hare, tortoise, peacock, partridge and scaly fish, may be eaten after being offered to gods and Brahmins. Meat may be eaten when consecrated by rite or when life is in danger, and one who refuses meat at a shraddha goes to as many hells as the animal has hairs. Liquor must never be drunk, touched or even looked at. One who eats or drinks what is forbidden goes to the Raurava hell.

02-018.json.summary: The sages ask Vyasa for a Brahmin's daily duties, and he gives them in order. Rising before dawn, the Brahmin thinks of dharma and meditates on the Lord, cleans his teeth with a twig and bathes in a river; the morning bath removes sins and bad dreams, and six lesser kinds of bath, such as with ash or by meditating on Vishnu, are allowed when one cannot bathe. He then offers water to gods, seers and ancestors, recites the Gayatri with Om, and performs the twilight worship (sandhya), meditating on Savitri in the sun; without it a Brahmin is impure and unfit for any rite. He recites the Savitri ten, a hundred or a thousand times and praises the sun with the Surya Hridaya hymn, which honours the sun as Brahman and as Rudra and removes all sin. At home he makes the fire offering, always with kusha and the sacred thread, worships the gods, serves his guru, studies and teaches the Veda, and then works to support his family. At midday he bathes again, cleaning himself with earth, remembering Narayana, and reciting the Aghamarshana hymn under water, which removes all sin as the horse sacrifice does. He offers flowers to the sun and recites sacred texts with a rosary, in silence, in a clean, lonely place. He then offers water to gods, seers and ancestors and worships Vishnu with the Purusha hymn, or Shiva with mantras such as 'Namah shivaya'. Then come the five great sacrifices: to the gods (fire offering), to beings (food on the ground for dogs, outcastes and birds), to the ancestors (feeding a Brahmin), to men (honouring guests, who are to be treated as the Lord) and to Brahman (study). Only then does he eat silently with his family. One who eats without these sacrifices goes to an animal womb, and one who eats without worshipping the gods is reborn among pigs; one who does them reaches the highest goal.

02-019.json.summary: Vyasa continues the daily duties of a Brahmin, now covering meals, evening and sleep. One eats seated facing east (for long life), south (fame), west (wealth) or north (truth), with hands, feet and mouth washed, the plate on clean ground; Manu says such a meal equals a fast. The food is circled with water while saying the great utterances (vyahritis), water is sipped as 'the nectar spread beneath', and five small offerings with Om and 'svaha' are made into one's own self to the five life breaths. The rest is eaten freely with the mind on the Lord; then water is sipped as 'the nectar covering', the heart is touched, and the self is joined to Brahman. This inner offering is called the highest of all sacrifices and leads to Brahman. Rules follow on eclipses and on not eating while others watch unfed or in anger; a life of eating only for oneself, sex only for pleasure and study only for a living is fruitless, and eating with head covered, facing north or with shoes on is called demonic. Many forbidden ways of eating are listed (at midnight or noon, in wet clothes, from a broken dish, lying down, with one's wife, in darkness or in temples, laughing or weeping). After eating one studies the epics and Puranas and performs the evening worship with the Gayatri; one who neglects the twilight worship is said to be like a Shudra. One sleeps with dry feet, not facing north or west, not naked, on a broken cot or in an empty house. A Brahmin who neglects these duties from disbelief or laziness goes to hell and is born a crow, for there is no path to liberation except one's own duties done to please the Lord.

02-020.json.summary: Vyasa teaches the times, places and foods for the rite for the ancestors (shraddha). The main monthly rite is done on the new-moon afternoon; the other days of the dark fortnight are also good, except the fourteenth. Other times are the ashtaka days of Pausha, Magha and Phalguna, the Magha full moon and harvest; occasional rites are required at eclipses and deaths of relatives, and optional ones give endless merit at solstices, equinoxes, the sun's entry into a sign and birthdays. The rewards of shraddha under each lunar mansion, weekday and lunar day are listed (for example sons, wealth, cattle, horses, learning or long life). The fourteenth gives bad offspring, so shraddha is done then only for those killed by weapons. Manu names five kinds of shraddha (daily, optional, occasional, prosperity and moon-phase), with a sixth for journeys, a seventh for purification and an eighth for gods. Places give endless merit: Ganga, Prayaga, Amarakantaka, above all Gaya (where the ancestors sing that one should have many sons in the hope that one goes to Gaya), Varanasi, Kurukshetra, Kedara, Naimisha, Pushkara, Narmada, Godavari and river banks generally. Pleasing foods include rice, barley, sesame, pulses, fruits and sugarcane. The ancestors' satisfaction from meat is graded from fish (two months) through deer, sheep, goat, boar and buffalo to cow's milk and milk-rice (a year) and the meat of the long-eared goat (twelve years). Foods to avoid include long pepper, lentils, gourds, brinjal, buffalo and goat milk, and black pepper.

02-021.json.summary: Vyasa explains which Brahmins to feed at the rite for the ancestors (shraddha). A Veda-learned Brahmin must be examined beforehand. Those who 'purify the row' (panktipavana) include soma drinkers, keepers of the fires, students of the four Vedas and special texts like the Rudradhyaya, knowers of the Puranas, worshippers of Mahadeva and devotees of Vishnu, those who never harm, yogis absorbed in Vedanta, and men not of the same gotra or family. The first choice is a calm yogi devoted to knowledge of truth, then a lifelong student, then a detached householder; feeding one such ascetic outweighs feeding a thousand Veda knowers. Relatives such as the maternal grandfather, uncle, daughter's son and teacher may be fed as a second option, but not a friend just to win him, nor an enemy. An unlearned Brahmin is like a straw fire; giving to him is like pouring into ashes, and he swallows red-hot iron balls after death. Six kinds of 'Brahmins only in name' (servants of Shudras or the king, husbands of Shudra women, village priests and others) are excluded, as are those who sell the Veda or teach for wages, and followers of Buddhist and Jain monks, Pancharatrins, Kapalikas, Pashupatas and other heretics. A long list of those who 'spoil the row' follows: those with skin disease or bad nails, thieves, unbelievers, drinkers, usurers, astrologers, musicians, the maimed, temple priests for pay, men ruled by their wives, sea travellers, the ungrateful, those who abandon parents, teacher or wife, mockers of gods, Vedas or Brahmins, and Brahmins who skip twilight worship or live on Shudra food.

02-022.json.summary: Vyasa gives the full procedure of shraddha. The day before, the ground is cleaned and Brahmins are invited; the ancestors, hearing of it, come swift as thought and eat with the Brahmins in airy form. Host and guests must stay chaste and calm and avoid travel and quarrels, with heavy punishments listed for breaking this. Next day kusha grass is brought, a secluded place sloping south is smeared with cow dung (one's own land or a holy place, not another's), and sesame is scattered and a goat tied to drive off demons. After midday the Brahmins are bathed and seated, two facing east for the All-gods and three facing north for the ancestors, or one each, since display harms the rite; a guest who comes must also be fed. The maimed, outcastes, heretics, a menstruating woman, and cocks, pigs and dogs are kept away. The gods are invoked and given arghya with barley; then, with sacred thread over the right shoulder, the ancestors are invoked with sesame water. Food is offered in the fire to Soma and Agni, or into a Brahmin's hand. Three rice balls (pinda) are set on kusha in a scored square and honoured. The Brahmins are fed meat, cakes and milk-rice in silence, served in gold, silver or udumbara vessels, never clay or iron; one who refuses meat at shraddha becomes an animal for twenty-one births. After they are satisfied, the host asks the ancestors for givers, Vedas, offspring and faith (this passage appears twice). The balls go to a cow, goat, Brahmin, fire or water, and a wife wanting a son eats the middle one; the couple stays chaste that night. A poor man may offer roots, fruits and sesame water. Rules follow for sons by appointed union, the yearly ekoddishta, and the prosperity rite (nandimukha), done in the morning to mothers, fathers and maternal grandfathers after worshipping the Mothers, who otherwise grow angry.

02-023.json.summary: Vyasa explains the rules of ritual impurity (ashaucha) after death or birth. For Brahmins it lasts ten days among close kin (sapinda), when daily rites and even silent study stop; it is shorter for those with learning and virtue, and a learned fire-keeper is pure at once, while a fool or neglecter of rites stays impure till death. Shorter periods apply for children who die before teething, tonsure or the sacred thread, for miscarriages, overlapping impurities and news of a distant death. Separate periods are given for unmarried girls, maternal grandfathers, in-laws, the teacher, a fellow student, the king and others. By class, a Brahmin is purified in ten days, a Kshatriya in twelve, a Vaishya in fifteen and a Shudra in a month, with mixed rules for relatives of other classes, carrying a stranger's body, or eating with the bereaved. Sapinda kinship ends at the seventh generation. Artisans, physicians, servants, students, ascetics, a consecrated king, and people at sacrifices, weddings or in famine are pure at once, as are those killed in battle, by lightning or snakes, or dying for cows and Brahmins. Outcastes and suicides get no cremation, impurity or shraddha, but an accidental death does. A fire-keeper is cremated with his fires; without a body, an effigy of palasha leaves is burnt. Kin offer water and a daily rice ball for ten days, shave on the second day, gather bones on the fourth, feed Brahmins on set days, and do the monthly ekoddishta for a year; then the sapindikarana rite joins the dead to the ancestors, after which a separate offering would make one a killer of his fathers. The son does these rites, else the wife, else a brother. Vyasa adds that the only dharma stated for women here is service to their husbands.

02-024.json.summary: Vyasa describes the householder's duty to keep the sacred fires. The fire offering (agnihotra) is made morning and evening, the new- and full-moon rites each fortnight, and the new-harvest, seasonal, animal and soma sacrifices at their times; a fire-keeper must not eat new grain or meat before offering them, or the hungry fires seek his life. One who out of disbelief or laziness does not keep the fires goes to hells such as Tamisra, Raurava, Kumbhipaka and the sword-leaf forest and is then born among outcastes or Shudras. There is no higher dharma for the twice-born than the agnihotra. One with three years' food for his dependants may perform the soma sacrifice, the first of all, worshipping Maheshvara with it. Brahma taught dharma in two forms, shrauta (tied to the Vedic fires, the more beneficial) and smarta (from the remembered texts); where both are silent, the conduct of the learned (shishta) decides. The Puranas and dharma texts expand the Veda, giving knowledge of Brahman and of dharma, so the twice-born should trust them.

02-025.json.summary: Vyasa explains how a twice-born householder may earn a living. Householders are striving (sadhaka) or non-striving (asadhaka). The first may teach, sacrifice for others and accept gifts, and in hard times farm, trade or lend through others; money-lending is sinful and to be avoided, and a Brahmin should take up the Kshatriya way before ploughing himself, never doing the ploughing in person. Profits should be shared: a farmer gives a twentieth to gods and ancestors and a thirtieth to Brahmins, a trader twice that and a lender three times. The non-striving householder lives by gleaning grain or single ears, or on what comes unasked ('immortal') or is begged ('dead'). Householders who store a granary, a jar, three days' food or nothing for tomorrow are each better than the one before. A Brahmin must live honestly and never by worldly tricks; one who earns wealth without satisfying gods and ancestors is born a dog. Of the four aims of life, a Brahmin may seek only desire that does not oppose dharma, and wealth is true wealth only when used for giving and sacrifice.

02-026.json.summary: Vyasa teaches on giving (dana); the chapter as printed starts at verse 2. Gifts are daily (expecting nothing), occasional (to remove sin), desire-driven (for children, power or heaven), and best of all pure (given to knowers of Brahman only to please the Lord). One gives what is left after family needs, to a learned, humble, poor Brahmin. Land is the highest gift, equalled by food and surpassed by teaching. Special gifts are described: on the Vaishakha full moon, honouring Brahmins with black sesame and honey for Dharmaraja wipes out a lifetime's sins; sesame on a black antelope skin, or sesame given on the twelfth of Magha, frees from great sins; gifts for Shiva on the new moon and on the dark eighth and fourteenth, and worship of Vishnu on the bright twelfth after fasting, bring the highest state. The gods dwell in Brahmins' bodies and are worshipped in images only when no Brahmin is found. Deities for each wish are listed: Indra for power, the Sun for health, Agni for wealth, Vinayaka for success, Hari for release, Maheshvara for yoga and liberation. Rewards of gifts follow: water brings contentment, a lamp good eyes, gold long life, a cow the sun's heaven, an umbrella and sandals safe passage through hell. Gifts at eclipses and holy places are endless. Those who block gifts become animals; a rich man who honours no Brahmins, or a Brahmin who withholds food in famine, should be banished by the king. One should not give to unbelievers or heretics, nor pass over a nearby worthy Brahmin. A Brahmin should take gifts only for his needs and never from a Shudra. A householder who worships the one Lord through household dharma is not born again.

02-027.json.summary: Vyasa describes the forest-dweller stage (vanaprastha). When he sees grandchildren and his body weakens, a man goes to the forest with his wife and fires, or leaves her with his sons. There he lives on fruits and roots, bathes three times a day, wears matted hair and bark, keeps the agnihotra and five great sacrifices with forest food, studies the Veda, harms none and accepts no gifts. He avoids honey, meat, mushrooms, ploughed-land grain and village produce, and stays strictly chaste; a child conceived in the forest has no right to the Veda. He sleeps on stone, lives with the deer, and stores food for a day up to a year, discarding it in Ashvayuja. Many hard ways of life are allowed: gleaning, eating only fallen fruit (the Vaikhanasa rule), the chandrayana fast, standing on tiptoe, the five fires in summer, wet clothes in winter, drinking only moonbeams, steam or milk. He practises yoga, recites the Rudradhyaya and studies Vedanta. Finally he takes the fires into himself, begs bare food, recites the Upanishads, and may set out on the great final journey, fast to death or enter fire. Those who follow this stage reach the Lord's supreme state.

02-028.json.summary: Vyasa describes the last stage of life, renunciation (sannyasa). Taking the fires into himself, the twice-born becomes a wandering ascetic, but only when true detachment has arisen, or he falls. Renunciants are of three kinds: by knowledge, by the Veda and by action; the one with knowledge is highest and needs no duty or outward sign. The ascetic owns nothing, wears an old loincloth or goes naked, eats little from begging, and waits for death like a servant for orders, welcoming neither life nor death. He may be shaven or keep a tuft, carry the triple staff, wear ochre, and live at a village edge, under a tree or in a temple, equal to friend and foe. He must never eat from one house only; for that the dharma texts give no atonement. He sees clay, stone and gold alike, harms nothing, steps where he has looked, drinks strained water and speaks only purified words. He stays in one place only in the rains, recites Om and the Vedanta, and keeps non-violence, truth, not stealing, chastity, austerity, patience, compassion and contentment. With water pot and triple staff, meditating on the Supreme Lord, the wise ascetic reaches the supreme.

02-029.json.summary: Vyasa continues on the renunciant (no speaker line opens the chapter). The ascetic begs once a day at up to seven houses, after the kitchen fires are out and people have eaten, stands eyes down, eats eight mouthfuls after offering to the life breaths, and uses a bowl of gourd, wood, clay or bamboo. At the night's watches and twilights he meditates on the Lord in the lotus of the heart: the source and self of all beings, bliss and imperishable light beyond nature, Mahesha shining like the rising sun, or Brahman as pure knowledge in the cave of the heart; this is called the most secret knowledge for ascetics. Penances for broken vows follow: for going to a woman, the santapana and a kricchra; for any lie, a fast and a hundred breath controls; for theft, called the worst wrong since wealth is a man's outer life, a year of chandrayana; for accidental harm, kricchra or chandrayana; for loss of semen, breath controls; for eating honey or meat, the prajapatya. Meditation destroys all sin. The text identifies Maheshvara with the one supreme Brahman; one who sees no god apart from Mahadeva and knows him as his own self reaches the highest state, while those who think themselves different from him toil in vain. This rule, first taught by Brahma, should be given only to a son, disciple or yogi.

02-030.json.summary: Vyasa begins the teaching on atonement (prayashchitta). Neglecting duties or doing forbidden acts brings fault, and a Brahmin must perform the atonement that calm, learned Brahmins declare, whether one fire-keeping scholar, three, seven or twenty-one experts. The great sinners are the killer of a Brahmin, the drinker of liquor, the thief of gold and the violator of his teacher's wife, along with those who live with them; a year's close contact with outcastes makes one an outcaste, and sacrificing for them, marrying into their family, teaching them or eating with them does so at once. The killer of a Brahmin must live in a forest hut for twelve years, bearing a skull as banner, begging once a day from seven houses while announcing his sin, carrying a skull and skull-staff and staying chaste. This is for unintended killing; for an intended one, purity comes only by death: fasting to death, falling from a cliff, entering fire or water, or dying for Brahmins or cows. Other means are curing a sick Brahmin, giving all one's wealth to a learned Brahmin, bathing at the end of a horse sacrifice, at the meeting of the Sarasvati and Aruna, or at Rameshvara. At Kapalamochana, where Bhairava set down Brahma's skull, bathing and worshipping Mahadeva as Bhairava frees one from this sin.

02-031.json.summary: The sages ask Suta how Rudra set down Brahma's skull on earth. Long ago on Meru, deluded by Shiva's maya, Brahma told the sages he was the supreme Lord and creator. A form born of Narayana laughed and claimed that title for himself. The four Vedas came and each declared that the supreme reality is Maheshvara, Rudra, Shankara. Brahma mocked: how could the supreme Brahman delight in a wife and proud attendants? Om itself took form and replied that the Goddess is Shiva's own bliss, not separate from him. Still their delusion lasted. Then a great light appeared in the sky; Brahma's fifth head blazed with anger, and the blue-red Lord (Nilalohita) appeared with a trident. When Brahma proudly told him to seek his refuge, the Lord sent forth Kalabhairava, who cut off Brahma's fifth head. Brahma died, was revived by the Lord's yoga, saw Shiva with the Goddess in the disc of light, regained true memory and praised them in the Somashtaka hymn. Shiva, pleased, told Nilalohita to spare Brahma but to carry his head and wander begging, to show the world the vow for the sin of killing a Brahmin. The terrible maiden Brahmahatya followed him until Varanasi. With the skull in hand, Bhairava roamed the worlds, followed by dancing women. At Vishnu's palace the doorkeeper Vishvaksena attacked him and was killed by a trident. Vishnu cut his own forehead and poured blood into the skull for a thousand divine years, but it never filled. Learning the story, Vishnu could not make Brahmahatya leave, so he sent Bhairava to Varanasi. As Bhairava entered the city, Brahmahatya cried out and sank to the underworld. There Shiva set down the skull, restored Vishvaksena to life, and declared that remembering his skull-bearing form destroys sin, that bathing there frees from killing a Brahmin, and that those who live there receive the highest state at death. This holy place is Kapalamochana, and reading the chapter frees from sins of speech, mind and body. (The verse numbering here is irregular.)

02-032.json.summary: Vyasa gives the atonements for the other great sins. A Brahmin who drank liquor must drink boiling liquor, or red-hot cow's urine, milk, ghee or water, until his body burns and he is freed, or keep the vow for killing a Brahmin. A thief of gold must go to the king with loose hair, carrying a club or iron rod, confess and ask to be punished; the king strikes him once, and he is purified by death or release, but a king who does not punish takes the sin. Alternatively he may keep the Brahmin-killer's vow, bathe at a horse sacrifice, give his weight in gold, or keep the kricchra for a year. One who violated his teacher's wife must embrace a red-hot iron image of a woman, or cut off his genitals and walk south until he dies; or keep the Brahmin-killer's vow, embrace a thorny branch for a year, or do several chandrayana fasts. One who associates with an outcaste must keep the same vow as the outcaste's sin requires. But for those who committed these great sins intentionally, the only atonement the sages saw is fasting to death or entering fire at a holy place while meditating on Shiva.

02-033.json.summary: Vyasa continues the atonements (no speaker line opens the chapter), first for sexual offences. Knowingly going to one's daughter, sister or daughter-in-law requires entering fire; for other close female relatives the penances range from the kricchra and atikricchra to several chandrayana fasts; for a friend's wife, a menstruating woman, a Chandala woman, a woman of one's mother's gotra, a maiden, a prostitute, an animal or women of various low occupations, specific fasts are set. A student who breaks chastity must wear a donkey's skin, beg at seven houses and confess his sin for a year. Penances for killing follow, graded by class: for a Kshatriya, six months of the Brahmin-killer's vow and five hundred cows; for a Vaishya and Shudra, less; for women of each class, eight, six, three and one years of the vow; for the lowest-born, a chandrayana. For animals there are set gifts or fasts: a sixteenth of the vow for a frog, crow or cat, a kricchra for a horse, an iron image for a snake, cows for various birds, a milk cow for flesh-eating beasts. For boneless creatures breath control suffices; cutting fruit trees needs a hundred Rig verses; killing a cow by accident needs a chandrayana, but for killing a cow on purpose there is no atonement.

02-034.json.summary: Vyasa completes his list of atonements and ends his teaching. Penances are given for stealing people, wells, food, metals, cloth and animals; for eating forbidden things such as human flesh, crow, dog, flesh-eating beasts, certain birds and fish, onion, garlic and mushrooms; for drinking forbidden milk or water touched by a Chandala; for eating at a new shraddha, outcastes' food or others' leftovers (graded by class); and for many other faults: letting the fire go out, missing twilight worship, unbelief, a Chandala reciting the Veda or Puranas, touching the dead or a menstruating woman, dog bites, rudeness to Brahmins or the teacher, and abusing gods (the tongue is burnt with a brand). For one who reviles Vishveshana, the lord of all beings, no atonement is possible even in a hundred years, yet by fasts and taking refuge in him he is freed. General purifiers include giving all one's wealth, visiting holy places, worship of Shiva on the new moon and dark eighth and fourteenth, sesame water to Yama and his names on the dark fourteenth, and fasting for Vishnu on the eleventh and twelfth. The text says a wife who enters the fire with her husband saves him even from great sin, calling this the highest atonement for women, and that a devoted wife can never be overcome. As an example, when Ravana came disguised to seize Sita, she prayed to Agni with an eight-verse hymn; Agni hid her, made an illusory Sita for Ravana to take, and after Ravana's death let the illusory one burn in the fire and returned the real Sita to Rama, telling him to know himself as Narayana. Vyasa says this dharma of Manu and the path of knowledge lead to Mahadeva, should be taught to calm, faithful Brahmins, and frees from sin when read at shraddha. He then comforted the sages and Suta and left. (The colophon calls this the thirty-third chapter while numbering it thirty-four.)

02-035.json.summary: The sages ask Romaharshana (Suta) to describe the great holy places (tirthas), where bathing, recitation, shraddha and gifts purify seven generations. Prayaga has already been praised. Kurukshetra cleanses all sins. At Gaya, where Rudra left his footprint on a rock, one pinda offering saves the ancestors, who sing that any descendant, even a sinner, who goes there will save them, so one should wish for many sons in the hope that one goes. Prabhasa gives Brahma's world; Traiyambaka gives the fruit of the jyotishtoma sacrifice; Someshvara cures disease; at Vijaya six months of discipline brings the highest state. Bathing in the Mahanadi at an eclipse or in the Viraja river frees from sin. Purushottama gives Vishnu's world; Gokarna and northern Gokarna give union with Shiva; at Kubjamra, Kokamukha, Shalagrama and Ashvatirtha Vishnu dwells. Pushkara, Brahma's holy place, gives Brahma's world. At Saptasarasvata, worshipping Rudra gives the fruit of a horse sacrifice. There the sage Mankanaka danced with pride in his austerity, so Shiva split his own body to show it was only ash, and danced in a terrible thousand-headed form with a radiant goddess beside him. The frightened sage asked what he had seen. Shiva explained that he is Time and the self of all, whose supreme maya is nature, that Narayana is the unmanifest in the form of maya, that Brahma creates when he joins spirit to nature, and that the goddess is his power of knowledge (Vidya); Vishnu, Brahma and Rudra all rest in the one Brahman, which should be worshipped with devotion. A learned Brahmin who visits this place is freed from all sins.

02-036.json.summary: Suta continues the holy places. Rudrakoti got its name when ten million sages came to see Shiva, each wanting to see him first; Shiva took ten million forms so that each saw him first, and they all longed for the highest state. Worship there brings nearness to Rudra; Madhuvana gives half of Indra's throne, and Pushpanagari saves a hundred generations. Kalanjara is where the royal sage Shveta, a devoted worshipper of Shiva, set up a linga and prayed constantly. Death (Kala) came with a spear to take him; the king clasped the linga and recited the Shatarudriya, but Death said no one escapes him and bound him with nooses. Then Shiva appeared with the Goddess in a blaze of light and asked for his devotee; when Death rushed at him, Shiva kicked him with his left foot and Death died. The king praised Shiva and was given leadership of his hosts and a form like his. At Brahma's request, Shiva let Death live again, since Death had only done the work given to him. One who worships Mahadeva at Kalanjara gains leadership of Shiva's hosts (ganapatya).

02-037.json.summary: Suta continues his list of holy places for the sages. At Mahalaya, a most secret shrine, Rudra left his footprint on a rock as proof for unbelievers; Pashupata ascetics smeared with ash worship there, and one who bathes and bows to the footprint comes near to Rudra. At Kedara, bathing, worshipping Shiva and drinking the water gives the rank of a leader of Shiva's hosts (ganapatya), and ancestor rites (shraddha) there give endless fruit. Many more places follow, each with a reward: Plakshavatarana, the Magadha forest, Kanakhala where Rudra destroyed Daksha's sacrifice, Mahatirtha, Shriparvata where Shiva lives with the Goddess, the Godavari and the Kaveri. Pilgrimage is said to be for the twice-born, with a fast of three nights or one, and its fruit comes only to one pure in speech and mind, self-controlled, free of greed and chaste. The list goes on with Svamitirtha where Skanda lives, the Tamraparni (offerings there save even sinful ancestors), Chandratirtha at the Kaveri's source, the Vindhyas, Dashashvamedhika, Pundarika, Brahmatirtha, Vinashana on the Sarasvati, the Yamuna's source, the peaks of Kubera, Uma and Bhrigu, Kurujangala, the Vaitarani, the Shraddha banyan, the Kaushiki and others, where gifts and shraddha never perish. At Mundaprishtha Shiva also left his footprint, and there a person sheds sin like a snake its old skin. Bathing in the Manasa lake wins half of Indra's seat. In the Himalaya the pond Sushumna frees a learned Brahmin from the sin of killing a Brahmin, and a shraddha there saves ten generations before and ten after; the whole Himalaya, the Ganga, rivers that reach the sea and the sea itself are holy. At Badari, where Narayana lives with Nara, one is freed from the stains of the Kali age. Last comes the Devadaru forest, where Shiva, after bewildering the sages and being worshipped by them, promised them success, lasting ganapatya to his worshippers there, no rebirth to those who die there, and freedom from sin even to those who remember it from afar; he lives there with Narayana, and every rite done there is endless. Wherever Shiva or Vishnu is, the Ganga and all holy places are present.

02-038.json.summary: The sages ask Suta how Shiva came to the Devadaru forest and bewildered the sages there. Suta tells how thousands of sages lived there with their families, busy with rites done for worldly ends. To show them the fault of this and teach the path of turning away from the world, Shiva came as a handsome naked young man of about twenty, golden and smiling, with Vishnu following him as a lovely dark woman in yellow clothes. Bewildered, the sages' faithful wives lost all shame and followed Shiva with desire, singing, dancing and trying to embrace him, while the sages' sons followed Vishnu in the same way. The angry sages cursed Shiva, but their curses failed against him like stars before the sun. He said he had come with his wife to do austerities; they told him to dress, leave his wife and then do austerities. Shiva asked how men who care for their own wives could ask him to leave his; they said a wife who goes astray should be left, and he replied that she never desired another even in thought. Calling him a liar, they drove him off. He went begging to Vasishtha's hermitage, where Arundhati washed his feet, treated the wounds the Brahmins had given him and asked who he was; he said he was chief of the perfected ones, blessed her and left. The Brahmins beat him with sticks, clods and fists and told him to tear off his linga; he did so, and at once he, Vishnu and the linga vanished. Terrible omens followed, and Anasuya told of a dream that Shiva with Narayana had come begging. Afraid, the sages went to Brahma and told him all. Brahma lamented that they had found and thrown away the greatest treasure, the one yogis and sacrificers seek. He explained that this was Mahadeva, beyond whom there is nothing, who as Time destroys and again creates all; his forms are Agni, Brahma and Vishnu, and his naked form is Brahman joined to yoga. The woman at his side was Narayana himself, the eternal supreme Self, into whose navel Shiva places the seed of creation, from which Brahma himself was born. Deluded by Shiva's maya, they had not known their own father; one should know him and take refuge in him for release. Marichi and the other sages, deeply troubled, question Brahma further. (The closing line in this edition calls it the forty-eighth chapter, though it is chapter 38.)

02-039.json.summary: The sages ask Brahma how they can see Shiva again. Brahma tells them to make a linga like the one that fell, and to worship it with their wives and sons under Vedic rules, setting it up with Shiva's Vedic verses and reciting the Shatarudriya; then they will see him. They return to the Devadaru forest and worship in many hard ways: living on moss, lying in water, standing on one toe, eating leaves, sleeping on rocks. To bless them Shiva comes again, ash-smeared, naked, a burning brand in hand, laughing, singing, dancing and begging, this time with Gauri at his side. The sages bow and praise him in a long hymn of salutations to the three-eyed, naked dancer, Bhairava, the half-man half-woman, the blue-throated, the bearer of the Ganga and the skull, the linga of gold, water, fire and knowledge, and ask forgiveness for what they did in delusion. Pleased, he shows his own supreme form with the Goddess. Bhrigu, Angiras, Vasishtha, Vishvamitra, Gautama, Atri, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, Marichi, Kashyapa and others ask how to worship him. Shiva says release comes through Sankhya (knowledge) joined with yoga: yoga alone does not reveal the supreme Person, while knowledge gives release. They had relied only on yoga, so he came to show their delusion. The Self is one, everywhere, pure consciousness and bliss; this knowledge is release. Calm ascetics devoted to him, smeared with ash, are soon carried across rebirth. One should keep the Pashupata vow he made as the secret essence of the Veda: calm, chaste, ash-smeared, naked or in a loincloth, studying the Veda and meditating on Pashupati. He says he also taught misleading scriptures opposed to the Veda, naming the Vama, Pashupata, Soma, Lakula and Bhairava systems, which are outside the Veda and not to be followed; he can be known only through the Veda. Promising to be near whenever they meditate on him, he vanishes. Later, as the sages debate the root of the world and the Self, the Goddess appears, bright as ten million suns and wrapped in flames. Seen by her, they see Shiva within her, and knowledge that ends birth rises in them: she is the womb of the world and Shiva's eternal power, not different from him, and knowing this brings immortality. Suta says that reading or hearing this story frees one from all sins.

02-040.json.summary: Suta repeats the greatness of the Narmada as Markandeya told it to Yudhishthira. Markandeya says the Narmada flowed from Rudra's body and saves all beings. The Ganga is holy at Kanakhala and the Sarasvati at Kurukshetra, but the Narmada is holy everywhere; the Sarasvati purifies in three days, the Yamuna in seven, the Ganga at once, and the Narmada just by being seen. It rises on Mount Amarakantaka in western Kalinga, where gods and sages won success by austerity; bathing there under rules and fasting one night saves a hundred generations. The river is said to be over a hundred yojanas long and two wide, with countless holy spots around the mountain. One who lives purely, harms no being, and dies there enjoys heaven for a hundred thousand years among nymphs and is then reborn a rich, righteous king; one who dies there by fire, water or fasting goes where there is no return. Offering rice balls at the lake Jaleshvara satisfies the ancestors for ten thousand years. On the south bank flow the Kapila, where even fallen trees touched by Narmada water reach the highest state, and the Vishalyakarani, which at once frees a bather from pain; fasting to death there leads to Rudra's world, and those living on the north bank live in Rudra's world. Bathing and giving in the Narmada equal the Sarasvati and Ganga. Placing its water on the head frees from all sins, and a day and night fast frees from the sin of killing a Brahmin. Visiting Amarakantaka during an eclipse gives ten times the merit of a horse sacrifice; Shiva lives there with the Goddess, with Brahma, Vishnu and Indra, and walking around the mountain gives the fruit of the Paundarika sacrifice. Bathing and worshipping Shiva where the Kaveri meets the Narmada brings honour in Rudra's world.

02-041.json.summary: Markandeya leads Yudhishthira along the Narmada from one bathing place to the next, naming the reward of each. On the north bank, Bhadreshvara brings joy among the gods, Amratakeshvara the fruit of a thousand cows, and Angarakeshvara, Kedara, Nishphalesha and Banatirtha lead to Rudra's world or fulfil all wishes; Pushkarini makes one a king and Shakratirtha gives half of Indra's seat. At Shulabheda a bath, a night's fast and worship of Narayana lead to Vishnu's world. Then come Narada's tirtha, where Shiva gave Narada yoga, the linga Brahmeshvara made by Brahma, Rinatirtha which frees from debts, Bhimeshvara which ends sickness, and Pingaleshvara, where one who gives a brown cow lives in Rudra's world for as many thousand years as the cow and its offspring have hairs. All who live on the Narmada's banks go to heaven. At Vyasatirtha the river once turned back in fear of Vyasa and flowed south at his angry cry. Further places include the meeting with the Ikshu, Skandatirtha, Angirasa, Kushatirtha, Kotitirtha, the Chandrabhaga, Sangameshvara and the Adityayatana, where even the poor, the sick and sinners reach the Sun's world. At Marudalaya a twice-born man who gives gold goes to Vayu's world; one who worships Ahalya on the bright thirteenth of Chaitra becomes loved by women like Kama; at Somatirtha the Chandrayana fast leads to the Moon's world, and one who enters fire or fasts in the water there is not born again as a mortal. Vishnutirtha at Yodhanipura, where Vasudeva fought demons, removes Brahmin-killing with a day's fast. At the Brahmatirtha called Umahaka, rice balls offered on the elephant-shaped rock, especially in Vaishakha, satisfy the ancestors as long as the earth lasts, and at Akolla rice balls at the tree's root satisfy them till moon and stars last. The greatest is Shuklatirtha, where Shiva lives with the Goddess and comes from Kailasa on the dark fourteenth of Vaishakha: as dyed cloth is washed white, it washes away a whole life's sins; bathing Shiva with ghee there on the dark fourteenth of Kartika keeps one with twenty-one generations in Shiva's abode, bathing ends rebirth, and helping a poor Brahmin marry there brings long life in Rudra's world. The list ends with Yamatirtha, the Erandi meeting (feeding one Brahmin equals feeding a crore), Kallolakeshvara, Nanditirtha, Anaraka (bathing saves from hell), Kapilatirtha with its rites on the fourteenth of Jyeshtha and on Tuesdays, Ganeshvara, Gangavadana, and Dashashvamedhika, where bathing and offering to the ancestors on any day gives the fruit of a horse sacrifice.

02-042.json.summary: Markandeya continues the Narmada pilgrimage for Yudhishthira. At Bhrigutirtha, where Bhrigu worshipped Rudra, seeing the god frees at once from sin, and those who die there are not born again; gifts of sandals, food and gold become endless, and Shiva, pleased by Bhrigu's austerity, promised to stay there. At Gautameshvara, where Gautama won success, bathing with a fast leads to Brahma's world. At Dhautapapa, where Shiva's bull washed itself, bathing removes the sin of killing a Brahmin, and one who dies there becomes four-armed and three-eyed, equal to Shiva in strength, and is later born sole ruler of the earth. Then come Hamsatirtha, Varahatirtha, Chandratirtha (bathing on the full moon makes one sole ruler of the earth), Devatirtha, Shankhitirtha (gifts multiply ten million times), the Paitamaha tirtha (shraddha becomes endless), Savitritirtha, Manohara, Kanyatirtha, Svargabindu and Apsaresha. At Bharabhuti, worship of Shiva in Kartika is worth ten horse sacrifices, giving a white bull leads to Rudra's world, and dying or entering the water there leads to Rudra's world or heaven. The meeting of the Erandi and the Narmada frees from Brahmin-killing, and bathing where the Narmada meets the sea, called Jamadagni, gives three times the fruit of a horse sacrifice. At Pingaleshvara fasting and seeing Vimaleshvara removes the sins of seven births, and a night's fast at Alikatirtha frees from Brahmin-killing. Markandeya says he has named only the chief places; they are too many to count. Merely remembering the Narmada gives the fruit of a hundred Chandrayana fasts, while faithless unbelievers fall into hell. Since Shiva himself always attends the Narmada, it takes away the sin of killing a Brahmin.

02-043.json.summary: Suta praises Naimisha, the holy place dear to Mahadeva. Long ago the sages of six families, the Marichis, Atris, Vasishthas, Kratus, Bhrigus and Angirases, asked Brahma how to see Shiva. Brahma told them to hold a sacrificial session (sattra) of a thousand months, free of faults of speech and mind, and released a wheel made of mind for them to follow: where its rim (nemi) wore away would be the place. That spot was named Naimisha. There the six families worshipped Shiva and saw him; every gift, austerity, bath or prayer there removes the sins of seven births; there the Lord once told the sages the Brahmanda Purana; Shiva still sports there with Rudrani; and twice-born who die there under vows reach Brahma's world and are not born again. Suta then tells of Japyeshvara, where Nandi recited Rudra's mantra. The sage Shilada worshipped Shiva for a son for a thousand years and asked for a son not born from a womb, free from death and equal to Shiva. Shiva agreed, and when Shilada ploughed his field a radiant boy rose from the earth calling him "father". Shilada did his birth rites and sacred thread and taught him the Veda. Nandi then resolved to conquer death, went to a holy river and recited the Rudra mantra ten million (a koti) times. Each time he finished a koti, Shiva came with Uma and offered a boon, and Nandi asked only to recite another koti; after the third, Shiva said there was no need. He made Nandi immortal and free of old age, always at his side, chief of his hosts, son of the Goddess, lord of yogis and all-knowing, holding Shiva's knowledge as clearly as a fruit in the hand. Shiva had him consecrated and himself married him to a famous daughter of the Maruts (her name is unclear in the text). A mortal who dies at Japyeshvara is honoured in Rudra's world.

02-044.json.summary: Suta names more holy places. Near Japyeshvara is Panchanada, where three nights' stay and worship of Shiva lead to Rudra's world. Then come Mahabhairava; the Vitasta river, which is Parvati herself; Panchatapa, where offerings to ancestors give endless fruit; Kayavarohana, where the sages set going the Maheshvara teachings and every rite becomes endless; Kanyatirtha; the tirtha of Rama son of Jamadagni (fruit of a thousand cows); Mahakala, where dying gives ganapatya; and the most secret Nakulishvara. At Gangadvara on the Himalaya Shiva lives with the Goddess and his disciples; bathing and worship there free from all sins. Bhimeshvara and the meeting of the Chandavega also remove sin. Above all is Varanasi, whose greatness was told earlier; release is not won elsewhere even by yoga in one birth. These chief places wash away the sins of hundreds of births. But one who gives up his own duties to go on pilgrimage gets no fruit in this world or the next. Pilgrimage is meant for one doing penance, a widower, a wandering householder and the like; a householder may go with his sacred fires or his wife, or after paying the three debts, arranging a living for his sons and placing his wife in their care. Suta says this greatness of holy places was told in connection with penance, and reading or hearing it frees one from all sins.

02-045.json.summary: Suta says the sages asked Kurma, Vishnu in tortoise form, to describe the dissolution of beings. Kurma names four kinds: the constant (nitya), the daily death of beings; the occasional (naimittika), the dissolution of the three worlds at the end of Brahma's day (a kalpa); the natural (prakrita), when everything from Mahat down to the elements is withdrawn; and the final (atyantika), the yogi's absorption in the supreme Self through knowledge. He describes the occasional one. After a thousand four-age cycles comes a hundred-year drought in which weak creatures perish. The sun's seven rays drink up the ocean and become seven blazing suns that burn the worlds until the earth is bare as a tortoise's back. The fire Samvartaka, driven by Kala-Rudra, burns islands, mountains and seas to ash, dries the underworld and burns the worlds Bhur, Bhuvar, Svar and Mahar with all their beings. Then huge roaring Samvartaka clouds of every colour rise, shaped like herds of elephants and lit by lightning, and for hundreds of years pour rain that puts out the fire, until the seas overflow, the mountains dissolve and the earth sinks. In that single ocean the Lord of beings sleeps in yogic sleep. The present kalpa is the Varaha kalpa; of the countless kalpas, sattvic ones show Hari's greatness, tamasic ones Hara's and rajasic ones Brahma's. The Varaha kalpa is sattvic, and Kurma says the sattvic kalpas are his, in which yogis worship Shiva and him and reach the highest state. He sleeps on the ocean, seen by the sages of Janaloka with the eye of yoga, and declares himself the ancient Person: the mantra, fire, Brahmins, cows, sacred grass, ladle, Soma and ghee, nature, time, the seed of the world, mother, father and Mahadeva; nothing exists apart from him, and yogis who know him reach immortality.

02-046.json.summary: Kurma tells the sages about the natural (prakrita) dissolution. When Brahma's lifetime of two parardhas ends, Maheshvara as the fire of Time enters the sun's disc and burns the whole cosmic egg, then hurls the Brahmashiras weapon into the bodies of the gods. Only the Goddess remains as his witness. Wearing a garland of the gods' skulls, the thousand-eyed Lord drinks the nectar of bliss and dances the Tandava looking at the Goddess, and she enters his body through yoga. Then each element dissolves into the one before it: earth into water, water into fire, fire into air, air into space, space into the first element-maker; the senses and gods merge into the forms of ego, ego into Mahat, and Mahat with Brahma into the Unmanifest. Maheshvara then separates nature (pradhana) and the Person (purusha); this dissolution comes from his will alone. He also grants the final dissolution to yogis whose minds rest in knowledge. Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva are the chief powers of the one supreme Self, and beyond them is the eternal trident-bearer, whom some call Agni, Narayana, Indra or Brahma; all gods are forms of the one Rudra, and Shiva gives fruit in whatever form he is worshipped. One should first worship him with form, three-eyed and seated in lotus posture (yoga with a seed); one unable to do so may worship Brahma, or else Vayu, Agni and Indra; best is to worship Shiva alone with devotion while keeping to one's duty. Vishnu as Vasudeva Narayana may be worshipped in the same way. Kurma says he taught this to Indradyumna and that the whole world is full of Brahman. The sages and Indra praise Kurma with a hymn naming Narayana, Krishna, Govinda, Varaha, Narasimha and Vamana. Suta then lists the contents of the whole Kurma Purana, from Lakshmi's birth and creation, through the unity of Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva, the Goddess, Daksha's sacrifice, royal lines, Krishna's life, the linga, Varanasi, Prayaga, geography, the Manu periods, the Ishvara Gita, penances and holy places, to the Devadaru forest, Nandi and the dissolutions. Vishnu then takes Shri, leaves the tortoise form and goes to his own abode. Rewards follow: reading it leads to Brahma's world; giving a written copy to a learned Brahmin in Vaishakha brings divine pleasures and later knowledge of Brahman; even one chapter frees from sins. It should be heard at shraddhas and sacrifices and outweighs all other Puranas and epics together. It must not be read near a Shudra (vrishala), and one who gives it to a faithless or unrighteous man goes to hell and is born a dog. The line of teaching runs from Narayana to Narada, Gautama and Parashara, and from Brahma to Sanaka and Sanatkumara, then Devala and Panchashikha, and from Sanatkumara to Vyasa, from whom Suta heard it. The Purana ends with salutations to Vyasa and to Vishnu in the tortoise form.
